prs.title: fix(plugins): run ralph-wiggum and output-style .sh hooks through bash with a quoted path
prs.body:
Refs #95673. Also fixes the ralph-wiggum / output-style half of #78490.

## What changes

Three bundled plugins registered their hook as a bare, unquoted script path:

| plugin | event | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ralph-wiggum` | `Stop` | `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stop-hook.sh` | `bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stop-hook.sh"` |
| `learning-output-style` | `SessionStart` | `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks-handlers/session-start.sh` | `bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks-handlers/session-start.sh"` |
| `explanatory-output-style` | `SessionStart` | same | same |

This is the form `security-guidance` already uses (`bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/sg-python.sh" …`). Each plugin's `version` goes 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 in `plugin.json` and in the `marketplace.json` entry, because the updater compares the `plugin.json` version: without the bump, existing installs stay on the cached 1.0.0 copy and never receive the new `hooks.json`.

## Why

Shell-form hook commands are handed to a shell (`sh -c` on macOS/Linux, Git Bash on Windows) with `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` exported, and the shell expands the variable. Three consequences of the bare form:

1. **Spaces in the plugin root break the hook on every platform.** Unquoted, the expansion word-splits, the shell tries to execute the first fragment, and the hook exits 127 with `not found`. For these three hooks that is silent: the output styles contribute no context and the ralph loop never continues. (#78490; a home directory like `C:\Users\Jane Doe` or `/Users/jane doe` is enough.)
2. **The bare form depends on the script's exec bit.** A delivery path that drops `+x` turns the hook into `Permission denied` (exit 126). `bash "<path>"` reads the script as data and does not care.
3. **On Windows the bare form leans on the CLI.** Current Claude Code prepends `bash ` to a hook command whose first word is a `.sh` file when it runs hooks through Git Bash (see the 2.1.161 changelog entry for #63828), so on an up‑to‑date CLI with Git Bash detected these hooks already get an interpreter — but still unquoted, so point 1 applies, and hosts on older CLIs get the file-association behaviour #95673 describes. Naming the interpreter in the plugin removes the dependency either way; the CLI leaves a command that already starts with `bash` untouched.

## What could break, and for whom

- macOS/Linux/Windows-with-Git-Bash users of these plugins whose plugin root has no space: no behaviour change; the same script runs under the same bash (`stop-hook.sh` is `#!/bin/bash`, the session-start handlers are `#!/usr/bin/env bash`).
- Users whose plugin root contains a space: the hooks start working after they update to 1.0.1.
- Windows without Git Bash (hooks default to PowerShell): these bash scripts could not run before and still cannot; the failure stays a non-blocking hook error.
- Rollback: revert this commit; nothing else reads these versions.

## Considered and deliberately not done

- **Exec form** (`"command": "bash", "args": ["${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/…"]`) avoids quoting entirely, but on Windows a bare `bash` spawned without a shell can resolve to WSL's `bash.exe` rather than Git Bash, and exec form needs a newer CLI than shell form. Shell form with quotes matches the existing convention.
- **`"shell": "bash"` on each hook** would turn the no-Git-Bash Windows case into an explicit "requires bash" error. Left out to keep parity with `security-guidance`; happy to add if preferred.
- **hookify's unquoted `python3 ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/…`** has the same word-splitting problem (and blocks every tool call when it hits). It already has two open PRs, #79644 and #81670, which also quote the three files here but keep the bare-path form; this PR supersedes their hunks for these three files only.
- **`/ralph-loop`'s `"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/setup-ralph-loop.sh"`** runs through the Bash tool, is already quoted, and is the subject of #80495; not touched.
- `ralph-wiggum`'s `stop-hook.sh` needs `jq`, which Git for Windows does not ship, so on Windows the Stop hook now launches correctly but still fails at `jq` when a loop is active. Separate problem; noted as a follow-up.
- The reporter's two follow-ups — a CI check that every bundled `hooks.json` command names an interpreter, and a plugin-docs note — are not in this PR. The hooks reference already says shell-form commands run through Git Bash on Windows; the lint is a reasonable follow-up and would be the regression guard this repo currently lacks for `plugins/*/hooks/hooks.json`.

## Verification

- All seven edited JSON files parse; `claude plugin validate` passes on the marketplace root and on each of the three plugins (the only warning is the pre-existing `security-guidance` entry/plugin.json version mismatch).
- Reproduced the failure and the fix the way the CLI runs shell-form hooks, with the plugins copied under a directory named `plugin root with space`:
  - before: `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT=".../plugin root with space/ralph-wiggum" sh -c '${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stop-hook.sh'` → exit 127, `sh: 1: .../plugin: not found` (same for both session-start hooks)
  - after: `sh -c 'bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stop-hook.sh"'` → exit 0; the session-start hooks emit valid `hookSpecificOutput` JSON (1018 and 3034 chars of `additionalContext`); with an active `.claude/ralph-loop.local.md` the Stop hook reads stdin and returns `{"decision":"block",…,"🔄 Ralph iteration 2 …"}`.
  - after, with `chmod -x stop-hook.sh`: still exit 0; the quoted-but-bare form from #79644/#81670 gives exit 126 `Permission denied` in that case.
- End to end with a real CLI (2.1.280-dev, Linux), loading each modified plugin with `--plugin-dir` from the spaced path in `-p` mode: the debug log shows `Hook SessionStart (bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks-handlers/session-start.sh") provided additionalContext (1018 chars)` and the model echoed the explanatory instructions; the unmodified copy logged `Hook SessionStart:startup (SessionStart) error: /bin/sh: 1: .../main: not found` and the model answered `NONE`. With ralph-wiggum and an active loop file, the log shows `Hook Stop (bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stop-hook.sh") returned permissionDecision: deny` and the loop advanced to iteration 2.
- Not checked on a Windows machine (none available here). The Windows claim rests on the CLI behaviour described above plus the reporter's own before/after in #95673.
- `plugins/plugin-dev/.../validate-hook-schema.sh` was tried and fails identically on `main` and on this branch (`jq: Cannot index string with number` — it does not understand the plugin wrapper format, #90292), so it is not a usable check here.
- This repo has no test harness for `plugins/*/hooks/hooks.json`, so there is no automated regression test in the diff; the interpreter-prefix lint above would be it.

prs.title: fix(hookify): make package import independent of the install directory name
prs.body:
Fixes #69665
Fixes #81448

## The problem

The hook entry points make the `hookify` package importable by putting
`os.path.dirname(CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT)` on `sys.path` and relying on the plugin
directory being named exactly `hookify`.

A marketplace install does not satisfy that — the plugin is unpacked into a
versioned directory (`.../hookify@0.1.0`), so `hookify` is not a name Python can
resolve there. Every hook event hits the `ImportError` branch and the plugin emits
`Hookify import error: No module named 'hookify'` instead of evaluating any rule.
The plugin looks installed but is inert, on every single hook event.

## Repro

With a real rule at `.claude/hookify.dangerous-rm.local.md` and input
`{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"rm -rf /"}}`:

```console
# plugin at .../hookify@0.1.0  (marketplace layout)
before: {"systemMessage": "Hookify import error: No module named 'hookify'"}
after:  {"systemMessage": "**[block-dangerous-rm]** ..."}
```

## The fix

Rather than inferring the package name from the directory layout, register the
package explicitly with its `__path__` pinned to the plugin root
(`hooks/_bootstrap.py`). That makes the import independent of the directory name.

It also removes the dependency on `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` being set and correct: the
root falls back to a path derived from `__file__` when the variable is missing or
does not point at a hookify checkout.

## Testing

- All four entry points (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, UserPromptSubmit) under a
  `hookify@0.1.0` directory.
- `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` unset — works.
- `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` pointing at a nonexistent path — works.
- Plain `hookify/` directory layout — unchanged, still works.

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Desktop App and Codex CLI (`codex exec`).

### What feature would you like to see?

Please add an opt-in **Include non-interactive sessions** filter to the Desktop App's chat history and search, so users can review persisted `codex exec` runs alongside interactive conversations.

Keeping interactive-only history as the default is reasonable. The missing capability is an explicit way to discover and inspect saved non-interactive work from the App, with a visible `exec` source badge to distinguish it from interactive chats.

Why this matters: users run Codex through terminal scripts or other orchestration tools, then return to the Desktop App to review what happened. A saved run that is absent from the App looks like missing history. Switching to chronological sorting does not make it appear, and there is no obvious explanation of the source distinction.

Suggested behavior:

- Add an opt-in filter covering persisted, non-archived `exec` sessions in history and search.
- Show the invocation source on these entries.
- Allow users to open the saved transcript for review.
- Keep ephemeral runs excluded and subagent visibility separately controlled.

### Additional information

I found the maintainer clarification in #16385 that `exec` and `codex_mcp` sessions are intentionally tagged separately from interactive sessions, and the request there to submit this as a feature request. This issue requests a visibility option; it does not claim the current exclusion is an unintended regression.

Local observations on 2026-11-03:

- Desktop bundle version: `26.1027.61615` (build `24141`, installed as ChatGPT.app).
- CLI: `codex-cli 0.166.0-alpha.5.1`.
- macOS `27.0.1`, Apple Silicon (`arm64`).
- A recent `codex exec` run has an existing rollout file and a row in the local state database.
- Sanitized metadata: `source=exec`, `thread_source=user`, `originator=codex_exec`, `archived=0`, `has_user_event=0`, `history_mode=paginated`.
- The run is absent from the App-provided recent/history lists inspected during troubleshooting.
- Changing the Codex sidebar to a flat list and sorting chats by `updated_at` was read back as applied, but the run remained absent from the recent list.
- These are observations of an existing run, not a fresh controlled reproduction. No database fields were modified, and no direct App resume of the run was tested.

Related: #42083 concerns a different lifecycle case, where an exec-origin thread was already resumed interactively in Desktop and then disappeared. #32614 concerns discovery of agent-created top-level tasks. This request is for explicit opt-in discovery of ordinary persisted non-interactive CLI runs.

Private paths, thread IDs, prompts, and transcripts are omitted.

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: context

issues.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

This report concerns regular consumer ChatGPT conversations (ChatGPT Plus). Newly started chats have repeatedly shown an Arabic warning for the maximum prompts allowed in that conversation after about 4–6 user messages. The next message cannot be sent. In one reported example at about 01:02 UTC on November 15, 2026, a fresh chat accepted five messages and rejected the sixth. This was the second consecutive affected chat. The exported transcript captures the exact warning:

> لقد وصلت إلى الحد الأقصى من المطالبات المسموح لك به لهذه المحادثة، ولكن يمكنك مواصلة التحدث عن طريق بدء دردشة جديدة.
>
> Translation: You’ve reached the maximum number of prompts allowed for this conversation, but you can keep talking by starting a new chat.

The same user also reports that multi-step tasks in regular ChatGPT increasingly return a final response after about 2–4 minutes with requested implementation or verification still outstanding. The user recalls previous tasks taking about 30–45 minutes. The model and thinking settings for those examples are unconfirmed. The two symptoms may have different causes.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start a fresh regular ChatGPT conversation in Chat mode. Record the client and model used.
2. Begin a multi-step task in Chat, then send successive follow-up messages. Repeat with short text-only prompts as a control.
3. Check whether the conversation rejects a follow-up after the first few messages and whether the task returned a final answer before its explicitly requested verification was complete.

This is the reported workflow. A controlled short-text-only reproduction and the exact model/reasoning preset for each affected run are still unknown.

### What is the expected behavior?

A new chat should accept follow-up messages within applicable limits. If a limit is legitimately exhausted, the UI should indicate which limit was hit and offer a way to continue. A task that stops before completing requested steps should surface the reason and which steps remain.

### Additional information

- The documented example is a 10-page exported transcript created at 01:01:50 UTC by Chrome 157 on Windows. It shows five user messages with assistant replies and a sixth user message followed by the warning, after a run displaying 4m26s. The export metadata identifies the export client. The client where the error first surfaced is still to be confirmed. The user also accesses ChatGPT from the Android app (1.2026.307).
- Plan: Plus.
- Similar reports: #61295 (Plus on web in a Project), #59432 (Pro on a new chat) and #55501 (premature limits in regular ChatGPT). This report adds an exact warning, verified turn count and timestamp. A shared cause has yet to be established.

Could maintainers route this to the team responsible for regular ChatGPT conversations and check the per-conversation prompt-limit counter, its relationship to context and plan usage, and task stop reasons?

issues.title: [Windows MXC / Codex CLI] Nested cmd.exe fails with ACCESS_DENIED under :root=deny; succeeds in :workspace

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
## Summary
A second `cmd.exe` process fails with `Access is denied` (exit code 1) when launched inside Codex's Windows MXC sandbox under a deny-by-default filesystem profile (`:root=deny`, `:minimal=read`), although the initial `cmd.exe` starts successfully. The identical nested-command check succeeds on the Windows host and in MXC with the built-in `:workspace` profile.

This is a **synthetic `codex sandbox` CLI test**, not an AI-agent session. No claim is made that this affects all MXC installations or all child-process mechanisms.

## Environment
- Windows 11 build **26100.9711**.
- Codex native CLI binary SHA-256: `9cbcc600be53a3aa18c1d55b36b462ebd2844ac16e24b991654774b0819599d5`.
- Codex MXC integration: `windows.sandbox=mxc`, invoked via `codex sandbox --include-managed-config --permission-profile ...`.
- No permanent Windows policy, ACL, Codex agent configuration, or network configuration changed.

## Restricted test profile
```toml
[permissions.jps225_strict]
extends = ":workspace"
filesystem = { ":root" = "deny", ":minimal" = "read", ":workspace_roots" = { "." = "write" } }
[permissions.jps225_strict.network]
enabled = false
```

Profile name is arbitrary. This configuration replaces the inherited filesystem map, leaving a narrow workspace write grant and basic runtime read permissions.

The host control is equivalent to:
```cmd
cmd.exe /d /v:off /c cmd.exe /d /v:off /c echo JPS225_CHILD_OK
```

MXC invocations use `codex sandbox -- ...` with the equivalent arguments: outer `cmd.exe /d /v:off /c` and nested `cmd.exe /d /v:off /c echo JPS225_CHILD_OK`.

## Controlled comparison (8 cases, all collected)

| Case | Exit code | Expected marker | Outcome |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Host initial cmd | 0 | present | PASS |
| Host nested cmd | 0 | present | PASS |
| MXC `:workspace` initial cmd | 0 | present | PASS |
| MXC `:workspace` nested cmd | 0 | present | PASS |
| MXC `:workspace` `SystemRoot` defined | 0 | present | PASS |
| MXC `:root=deny` initial cmd | 0 | present | PASS |
| **MXC `:root=deny` nested cmd** | **1** | **absent** | **ACCESS_DENIED** |
| MXC `:root=deny` `SystemRoot` defined | 0 | present | PASS |

A subsequent independent check reproduced the strict-profile nested-command failure once more (exit code 1, `Access is denied`, no child marker). The reproduced check did not use the AI agent.

## Native Windows event correlation limits
Six already-existing Windows event channels were queried during the second reproduction. Five channel queries returned exit code 0 but their XML could **not be parsed by the collector**; the sixth was unavailable or inaccessible (RC 15007). No attributable native-denial event was obtained.

**This does not prove that Windows did not record the denial**. No audit collection was enabled, and no event content was exported.

## Questions for maintainers
1. Is nested native process creation expected to work with `:root=deny`, `:minimal=read` and a narrow workspace write grant in Codex's MXC integration?
2. Does `:minimal=read` cover executable image mapping, DLL dependencies and directory traversal for descendants? Are there documented *narrow* grants required, without broadening the filesystem root?
3. Is blocked-denial tracing (such as `captureDenials.mode=block`, or a supported equivalent) accessible through `codex sandbox` while enforcement remains active?
4. Is this more likely a Codex permission-profile translation issue or Windows ProcessContainer behavior? Which native diagnostic or version mapping can establish that distinction?
5. Is there a verified configuration or fix preserving deny-by-default filesystem access, disabled direct network egress and inherited restrictions for child processes?

## Safety and scope
- The `:workspace` profile was used **only as a diagnostic positive control**, not as an approved production security policy.
- This is not a proof of a universal MXC weakness or inability to create child processes.
- No AI-agent execution or complete isolation attestation occurred.
- No private paths, user identities, repository contents, tokens, raw event logs, or WIP inventory are included.
- Related but distinct reports: #55032 (root deny and explicit filesystem grants) and #59152 (SYSTEMROOT issue under deny policies). In this reproduction `SystemRoot` was present in both MXC profiles.

I can provide further sanitized test output or a minimum reproduction trace upon request.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

issues.body:
## Summary

Codex in the macOS desktop app repeatedly fails with HTTP 400 and `{"detail":"Bad Request"}` while continuing a long-running task. Successful tool operations can be followed by a failed model-continuation request. The UI then shows the generic error and the goal becomes blocked. Retrying/resuming sometimes makes progress before the error recurs.

This report summarizes diagnostics captured on October 30, 2026. It is not a minimal deterministic reproduction, and the backend rejection reason is unknown.

## Environment at the time of failure

- ChatGPT desktop app: `26.1027.30824`
- Bundled Codex CLI: `0.166.0-alpha.5.1`
- macOS: `15.5`, build `24F74`
- Model in failed requests: `gpt-6-astra`
- Reasoning effort: `xhigh`
- Transport recorded locally: `responses_http`, HTTP/1.1

## Observed sequence

1. Continue an existing long-running task involving local tool operations.
2. A tool completes successfully and its matching response is present in the local session record.
3. The subsequent model-continuation request to `POST https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses` returns HTTP 400.
4. The UI displays only `{"detail":"Bad Request"}`; work is interrupted and the goal is shown as blocked.
5. Resume/retry. Some operations succeed, but the error recurs. Reducing work to individual small tool calls did not eliminate it.

One confirmed occurrence followed a file-save operation; another followed read-only diagnostics. The failure is therefore not observed exclusively after an editing-app mutation. Saved local work remained intact.

## Two confirmed failures for server-side correlation

| Failure time (UTC) | America/Los_Angeles time | HTTP status | x-oai-request-id |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-30 19:59:35 | 2026-10-30 12:59:35 PDT | 400 | `4dcae5bc-69a7-4286-8c75-578144d31e1f` |
| 2026-10-30 19:55:21 | 2026-10-30 12:55:21 PDT | 400 | `a5feda72-047d-4a5b-978b-4752c152bdf7` |

Both returned the same generic JSON error from the endpoint above.

## Diagnostic observations, not a root-cause claim

- Available local debug/trace diagnostics provide request IDs but no rejected field or actionable backend validation reason.
- The latest failed request was recorded as 43,836,758 bytes before zstd compression and 1,724,026 bytes after compression. Immediately preceding requests of almost the same size succeeded. Request size is a possible factor, not an established cause.
- The local core reported 197,439 tokens, below its configured 244,800 auto-compaction threshold and 258,400 full-context limit; local limit-reached flags were false. These figures do not establish how the server evaluated the request.
- This report does not establish media corruption, an external-tool failure, or a specific context-limit bug.

## Expected behavior

Continue after successfully completed tool operations, or provide an actionable validation error and supported recovery path. A generic HTTP 400 should not repeatedly strand the user without identifying what can safely be retried or changed.

## Requested investigation

Please correlate the two request IDs, identify the rejected field or server condition, and advise a supported workaround. Please also investigate the client experience: only a generic error is displayed and the goal repeatedly becomes blocked after successful work.

Potentially related symptom reports: #55930 and #57874. They concern other environments; a common cause has not been established.

## Privacy

Only this sanitized summary is shared. Email, conversation and turn identifiers, local paths, raw logs, prompts, session transcripts, credentials and project media are intentionally omitted. No attachments are included.

labels.name: bug

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
### Summary

After exiting Codex CLI in Ghostty, mouse wheel / trackpad scrolling stops working in `less` in the same terminal tab. Scrolling works normally before running Codex.

I observe this when exiting with either Ctrl-C or `/quit`. I could not reproduce the problem in Terminal.app.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open a fresh Ghostty terminal tab.
2. Run `seq 1 200 | less` and verify that mouse wheel / trackpad scrolling works.
3. Quit `less`, then launch `codex`.
4. Exit Codex using Ctrl-C or `/quit`.
5. Run `seq 1 200 | less` again.
6. Observe that mouse wheel / trackpad scrolling no longer works.

### Expected behavior

Exiting Codex should restore the terminal's previous scroll mode so that subsequent applications behave as they did before launching Codex.

### Actual behavior

Mouse wheel / trackpad scrolling stops working in `less` after Codex exits.

### Workaround and diagnostic finding

Quit `less` and run:

```sh
printf '\033[?1007h'
```

Then reopen `less`. Scrolling immediately works again. I have manually tested this workaround.

This suggests that DEC private mode 1007 (alternate scroll) is left disabled after Codex exits.

### Possible cause

In Codex CLI 0.169.0, `release_input()` unconditionally emits `DisableAlternateScroll` during alternate-screen cleanup. This may disable Ghostty's initially enabled alternate scroll mode without restoring its previous value.

Source inspected for this hypothesis is available in [alternate_screen.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.169.0/codex-rs/tui/src/tui/alternate_screen.rs#L174-L208).

[Ghostty issue #641](https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/issues/641#issuecomment-1753310907) provides relevant background. The maintainer explains that `less` relies on alternate scroll for wheel scrolling and that Ghostty enables this mode by default.

The cause remains a hypothesis based on the successful workaround and source inspection.

### Environment

- Codex CLI 0.169.0
- Ghostty 1.4.0, build 18457
- macOS 15.7.1
- Architecture arm64
- Comparison terminal Terminal.app, where I did not reproduce the problem

### What issue are you seeing?

A gold/yellow border remained around the user's display after a Codex chat had finished its native desktop capture work. Investigation found the Windows Computer Use helper still running and its Windows capture-access record still open approximately five hours after the screenshot-producing turn completed.

The request is for capture resources to be released when their owning work ends, while preserving Computer Use for other chats that actually need it.

#### Verified incident timeline

Times below are UTC, with America/New_York (UTC-04:00) equivalents. Incident date was October 25, 2026 locally.

| UTC | Local time | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-10-25 19:58:05.097 | Oct 25, 15:58:05 | The originating chat called `driveClient.getScreenshot()` on a Google Drive desktop window during an authorized backup/restore verification. |
| 2026-10-25 19:58:07.456 | Oct 25, 15:58:07 | Windows CapabilityAccessManager's entry for this helper records capture-access start. |
| 2026-10-25 20:02:51.338 | Oct 25, 16:02:51 | Another `driveClient.getScreenshot()` call occurred in the same turn. |
| 2026-10-25 20:04:50.622 | Oct 25, 16:04:50 | The local transcript records `task_complete` for that screenshot-producing turn. |
| Before 2026-10-26 01:04:26 | Before Oct 25, 21:04:26 | The user reported the persistent gold display border. The helper remained running; its capture-access stop time was still zero. Latest inspected turns of active chats were using files, APIs, or browser automation, with no current native desktop-capture calls found in those turns. |
| 2026-10-26 01:04:26.466 | Oct 25, 21:04:26 | Only the positively identified stale `codex-computer-use.exe` helper was terminated. Windows then recorded a nonzero capture-access stop time. |

The completion timestamp comes from the original transcript's lifecycle event, not an assumption based on the chat appearing idle.

#### Process and Windows evidence

- The retained process was `codex-computer-use.exe`, PID 34140, directly parented by the main `ChatGPT.exe` process, PID 48532.
- Its command line was the bundled helper path followed by `--parent-pid 48532`.
- Loaded modules included `GraphicsCapture.dll`, `Windows.Graphics.dll`, `d3d11.dll`, and `dwmapi.dll`.
- A separate `codex-computer-use-swift.exe` helper was present and was left untouched.
- The relevant Windows record was under:
  `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\CapabilityAccessManager\ConsentStore\graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder\NonPackaged\<encoded-helper-path>`.
- Before cleanup: `LastUsedTimeStart = 134374318874561759`, `LastUsedTimeStop = 0`.
- After cleanup: `LastUsedTimeStop = 134374502664667304`, corresponding to `2026-10-26T01:04:26.4667304Z`.
- After cleanup, the old helper was absent; no replacement `codex-computer-use.exe` was observed in the follow-up checks. The main app and both checked Codex agent-server processes remained running, and ongoing chats continued.
- No app restart, broad process kill, plugin disablement, or Windows permission change was used.

The user-visible border was reported by the user. The verified post-cleanup result is helper termination plus Windows recording capture access as ended; no new desktop screenshot was taken merely to verify the border.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is one observed incident sequence, not a verified deterministic minimal reproduction:

1. Run multiple chats in the Windows desktop app with Computer Use enabled.
2. Have one chat capture a native application window using Computer Use.
3. Let the screenshot-producing chat turn complete, and continue ordinary work in other chats.
4. Observe whether the gold/yellow capture border and native helper persist after native desktop work has ended.
5. Check the helper's Windows capture-access record for an unset stop time.
6. In this incident, terminating only the identified stale native capture helper caused Windows to record the end of capture access while the app and other chat agents remained running.

Please do not use a blanket helper-killing rule as the product fix: another chat may legitimately be using the same helper.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Release native capture sessions, cached frames, and associated graphics resources promptly when the owning chat finishes or relinquishes desktop use.
- Remove the Windows capture indicator when no capture remains needed.
- Preserve any other chat's active native operation.
- Allow a later authorized Computer Use task to acquire a fresh session normally.
- Handle ordinary completion, interruption, errors, disconnects, and concurrent chats.

### Additional information

#### Existing cleanup and a possible lifecycle ordering gap

Local, read-only inspection found that cleanup mechanisms are already present:

- User configuration already had a `notify = [<bundled codex-computer-use.exe>, "turn-ended"]` entry.
- The installed unified-computer-use MCP configuration included its hidden `turn_ended` tool.
- The shipped Windows client registers an `addTurnEndedHandler` and sends an `end_turn` request.
- The shipped desktop JavaScript tracks active turns by native-pipe socket. Its `end_turn` path removes matching active-turn entries. Separately, `closeActiveTurn` first checks that tracking map and returns without closing the helper transport if the turn is no longer present.

**Hypothesis, not a confirmed root cause:** if the end-turn request removes ownership tracking before the outer `turn/completed` cleanup checks it, the later cleanup could skip closing the helper transport, allowing cached capture resources to outlive the turn. Please investigate the interaction between the end-turn callback, socket/turn ownership tracking, helper transport closure, and the native capture cache.

This was static inspection of the installed JavaScript plus process/registry observations. No instrumented race reproduction or native decompilation established the exact defect.

#### Scope and limitations

- The persistent border, retained graphics-capture helper, original turn-completion timestamp, open Windows access record, and successful targeted cleanup are the evidence being reported.
- The registry record alone does not prove continuous frame acquisition, video recording, uploading, or continuous model access to the display. No such claim is made here.
- Later native activity in other turns is not exhaustively ruled out. At diagnosis, no current native capture calls were found in the latest turns inspected.
- No full transcripts, screenshots, credentials, account email addresses, personal usernames, or unrelated project content are included.

Related, but a different primary symptom: #56941 reports a retained helper after Computer Use on the same desktop package version, with system-wide UI lag. This report concerns the lingering capture indicator and capture-access lifecycle; a common cause is not established.

Also related: #46675 describes the takeover overlay remaining until the entire agent turn ends on an older build. The present incident includes a verified completed screenshot-producing turn and Windows capture access remaining open afterward, rather than only an overlay persisting during the same active turn.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Windows application package `OpenAI.Codex` version `26.1027.3384.0` (read from the installed Windows package metadata; the About dialog version was not separately checked).

### What subscription do you have?

Paid subscription; exact tier was not recorded.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64.

### What issue are you seeing?

Browser control repeatedly failed during a **Codex** desktop task with this exact error:

```text
Local browser use is disabled in Work settings
```

The user reported that browser access was enabled, explicitly authorized browser operation, opened the target site in Edge and Chrome, signed in, and supplied a correct tab mention. A screenshot confirmed that the intended signed-in page was open. The error nevertheless prevented the agent from even listing browser tabs. The reference to "Work settings" during a Codex task also caused considerable confusion and repeated, unhelpful requests to check already-enabled settings.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed on 2026-11-03 in a Windows desktop Codex task:

1. Open and sign into the intended website in Edge or Chrome, then authorize the task in Codex.
2. Ask the agent to use the open browser tab; a specific user-shared tab mention was also tried.
3. The exposed browser tools repeatedly returned the error above, including these calls:

```javascript
await cua.listTabs({ browser: "edge" });
await cua.listTabs({ browser: "chrome" });
await cua.getBrowser({ id: "iab" });
await cua.getState();
```

For `getState()`, the native application inventory could see running Microsoft Edge with the correct site in its window title, while the browser inventory returned:

```json
{
  "browsers": [],
  "errors": [
    "Browsers: Error: Local browser use is disabled in Work settings"
  ]
}
```

The failures recurred across turns and after resetting the browser-tool JavaScript session.

### What is the expected behavior?

Browser access in Codex should use the applicable desktop/session permissions. If it is blocked, the error should accurately identify the controlling setting or connection problem, rather than leaving the user and agent to infer that the task is running in Work or that browser permission was never enabled.

### Additional information

This appears intermittent or dependent on connection state. Later in the same task, a normal `cua.getTab({ url: "<the already-open target URL>" }, { browser: "edge" })` call succeeded, returned the Edge extension binding and the correct page, and browser operations then worked. Earlier tab-mention access had also failed. We do not know what changed and cannot establish the root cause or a reliable recovery procedure.

The operation was eventually completed through the normal browser and connected service tools. No browser security warning or permission setting was bypassed. Please investigate the browser permission/session check and the misleading product-specific error text.

The target URL, private project identifiers, account details, screenshots containing session URLs, and credentials are intentionally omitted from this public report.

issues.title: Windows desktop app: workspace routing discovery failed (HTTP 432) after successful OAuth login
issues.body:
The Windows ChatGPT/Codex desktop app successfully completes OAuth login but cannot load workspace settings or account data.

The application displays:

Workspace routing discovery failed

Workspace routing is unavailable

Unable to load workspace settings

Multiple requests fail with HTTP 432.

Environment

OS: Windows 11

Locale: ja-JP

Country: Japan (supported region)

Desktop app: OpenAI.Codex 26.1027.3384.0 (from logs)

Codex CLI: 0.166.0-alpha.5.1

Antivirus: Norton

Anaconda installed, with (base) automatically activated in PowerShell

Steps to reproduce

Launch the Windows desktop application.

Sign in successfully using ChatGPT OAuth.

Wait for workspace settings and account data to load.

The app reports a workspace loading failure.

Retry. The same error occurs.

Actual behavior

The desktop logs repeatedly show:

status=432 errorMessage="Workspace routing is unavailable"

Affected routes include:

/settings/user

/profiles/me

/accounts/check/v4-2023-04-27

/accounts/optimized/check

/accounts/verified_access

/wham/usage

/pins

Other logged errors:

workspace routing discovery failed

account/read errorCode=-32603

accountsHttpStatus=0

authenticatedAccountPresent=false

http/request send failed

error_is_connect=true when connecting to https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/ps/mcp

Network diagnostics

An unauthenticated GET request to:

https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/ps/mcp

returns:

HTTP 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons

SSL verification result: 0

Server: cloudflare

x-openai-proxy-wasm: v0.1

The same HTTP 451 is returned using both home Wi-Fi and smartphone tethering on the Windows PC.

An unauthenticated HEAD request also returns HTTP 451.

A smartphone browser using cellular data displays:

{"message":"no_biscuit_no_service"}

The smartphone HTTP status was not measured. These curl requests did not include browser authentication cookies and therefore do not reproduce the desktop application's authenticated POST request.

Request identifiers

GET request:

Timestamp: 2026-10-31 01:09:14 UTC

x-oai-request-id: d355e346-62fc-4626-bbd7-9d0666cbd886

CF-RAY: a52ec5ef98bd8323-KIX

HEAD request:

Timestamp: 2026-10-31 01:23:01 UTC

x-oai-request-id: 4f994b82-a0c7-4cec-9f1e-70d01965dd09

CF-RAY: a52eda202d4ad3f7-KIX

Certificate environment findings

Initially, both Codex CLI and the desktop app failed OAuth token exchange.

The CLI login succeeded after:

Setting CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE to C:\ProgramData\anaconda3\Library\ssl\cacert.pem

Removing the process-level SSL_CERT_FILE variable

Subsequently, setting CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE at the Windows user level enabled successful desktop login.

The Codex Doctor connectivity checks initially failed. After removing SSL_CERT_FILE from the PowerShell process, they passed:

WebSocket connected: HTTP 101 Switching Protocols

Active provider endpoints reachable over HTTP

No connectivity failures

However, the desktop app continues to fail workspace routing even after Windows sign-out and sign-in.

Expected behavior

After successful OAuth login, the Windows desktop application should load workspace settings, account information, and project data.

Additional notes

Browser ChatGPT works.

Reinstall/repair and alternate network tests had previously failed to resolve the login issue.

The effect of Norton's HTTPS/TLS inspection has not been conclusively tested.

It is not established whether HTTP 451 and the desktop HTTP 432 share the same root cause.

Please investigate the desktop workspace routing discovery failure and whether the certificate environment variables or route-aware HTTP client influence this behavior.

A fix preserving existing local Codex sessions and data would be appreciated.

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

App, CLI

### What feature would you like to see?

Title: Support message validation, non-blocking feedback, and request-scoped developer instructions through hooks.json

## Related issue

#33420 requests a MessageDisplay hook for observing streamed assistant output:
https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/33420

This request adds validation before display, feedback for subsequent output, and request-scoped developer instructions.

## Problem

I want to apply local policies to assistant commentary.

The Stop hook runs after commentary has already been displayed. An observational streaming hook cannot reject a message before display or provide structured feedback for the next model request.

Policies may use regular expressions or local classifiers, without calling another LLM for every message.

For some violations, I want to display the current message unchanged and guide subsequent output. Other policies may require an immediate rewrite.

## Requested MessageDisplay hook

Support a MessageDisplay event in hooks.json, with a matcher for the message phase, such as commentary.

The hook should receive the complete message text, phase, and session/turn/item identifiers.

Proposed results:

- `passed: true` — display the original message.
- `passed: true` with a nonempty `reason` — display the original message and queue the feedback for the next model request in the same session.
- `passed: false` with a nonempty `reason` — ask the model to rewrite the message before displaying it.

Example non-blocking feedback:

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "MessageDisplay",
    "passed": true,
    "reason": "For subsequent output, retain necessary facts and evidence and omit unrelated assurances or self-explanation."
  }
}
```

For non-blocking feedback:

- Keep the current message unchanged in display and replay.
- Add the feedback as developer context to the next model request.
- Apply it once, without permanently appending it to conversation history.
- Do not trigger an additional model request solely to deliver feedback.

For matching messages:

- Buffer text until validation completes.
- If rewriting is required, apply the approved message consistently to deltas, completion events, and conversation replay.
- Rewrite only the message; do not repeat tool executions.
- If the hook is unavailable, times out, or returns an execution error, display the original message and log the error.

## Request-scoped developer instructions

Allow PreModelRequest to return an optional developer instruction and an enable/disable state.

A local policy service could dynamically control instruction injection and message validation:

- Enabled: inject the configured instruction for this request and validate its commentary.
- Disabled: omit the instruction and skip validation for subsequent requests.

Instructions must apply only to the current request. Turning a policy off should also stop applying its queued feedback.

Example proposed response:

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PreModelRequest",
    "enabled": true,
    "developerInstruction": "Report concrete findings and results concisely."
  }
}
```

## Proposed hooks.json configuration

Reuse existing hook handlers, including mcp_tool, with an already-configured MCP server:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreModelRequest": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "mcp_tool",
            "server": "local-policy",
            "tool": "prepare_request"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "MessageDisplay": [
      {
        "matcher": "commentary",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "mcp_tool",
            "server": "local-policy",
            "tool": "review_message",
            "input": {
              "text": "${text}",
              "phase": "${phase}",
              "session_id": "${session_id}",
              "turn_id": "${turn_id}",
              "item_id": "${item_id}"
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Event fields and response fields above are proposed interfaces.

## Expected scope

Support the shared Codex Core path so the CLI and App Server behave consistently.

Users should be able to configure this through native hooks while retaining Codex's existing login and model connection.

issues.body:
Importing one Claude Code MCP server through the app server rewrites the entire existing `.codex/config.toml`. The import reports success, but setup notes and commented-out settings elsewhere in the file disappear.

**Environment**  Codex CLI 0.169.0, Linux x86_64. Reproduced in a disposable local Git repository with a fresh Codex home. No model request or live MCP server is needed.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Initialize an empty Git repository and create `.codex/config.toml` with these contents:

   ```toml
   # NOTE: retain these project-specific setup instructions.
   # model = "other-model"
   model = "gpt-5.4" # current selection
   ```

2. Create `.mcp.json` at the repository root:

   ```json
   {"mcpServers":{"demo":{"command":"echo","args":["demo"]}}}
   ```

3. Start `codex app-server --stdio` in the repo. Send `initialize` with `{"clientInfo":{"name":"repro","version":"1"},"capabilities":{"experimentalApi":true}}`, then the `initialized` notification.
4. Call `externalAgentConfig/detect` with `{"includeHome":false,"cwds":["<absolute repo path>"]}`. Pass its returned `items` array to `externalAgentConfig/import` as `migrationItems`.
5. Wait for `externalAgentConfig/import/completed`, then read `.codex/config.toml`.

**Observed**  The completion notification lists `demo` under successes with no failures. The entire file now reads:

```toml
model = "gpt-5.4"

[mcp_servers.demo]
command = "echo"
args = ["demo"]
```

**Expected**  Add `mcp_servers.demo` while preserving the existing config text, including comments and disabled settings. In an unversioned config those notes can be difficult to recover.

**Suggested fix**  Merge the new entries into a formatting-preserving TOML document and check the untouched portion byte-for-byte in a regression test. The import currently deserializes the entire file into `toml::Value` and serializes it again. Related issue #45432 covers `codex mcp add/remove`; this reproduction uses the external-agent migration handler. [Import code](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/de83e7674a69b9ae18544dd1fbf53f31bfe8c640/codex-rs/external-agent-migration/src/service.rs#L646-L655)

issues.title: require_escalated approval does not disclose retained network policy during partial escalation

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.169.0`

### What subscription do you have?

Pro

### Which model were you using?

Not relevant; this concerns command approval and sandbox policy.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS on Apple silicon, using Codex Desktop.

### What issue are you seeing?

When a custom permission profile contains denied-read filesystem entries, an explicitly approved `require_escalated` command uses the partial-escalation path that retains filesystem protections. Current behavior also retains the owner-managed network allowlist.

The security behavior appears intentional, but the approval contract does not disclose it:

- the tool schema describes `require_escalated` as “unsandboxed execution”;
- Codex asks the user to approve escalation;
- the user approves;
- the command remains subject to the owner network allowlist;
- the command then fails with an allowlist error.

Example error after approval:

```text
Network access to "api.doppler.com" was blocked: domain is not on the allowlist for the current sandbox mode.
```

The same session reproduced this with Codex's own management CLI against `ab.chatgpt.com` and a nested `codex exec` attempt against `api.openai.com`.

The active profile intentionally had:

- workspace writes;
- denied-read globs for `**/.env` and `**/.env.*`;
- managed networking enabled;
- only loopback domains in the allowlist.

The equivalent third-party command reached its service from the user's normal terminal, confirming this was the effective Codex policy rather than host connectivity.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure a permission profile with a denied-read entry and a limited managed-network domain list:

```toml
default_permissions = "coding"

[features]
network_proxy = true

[permissions.coding]
extends = ":workspace"

[permissions.coding.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
"**/.env" = "deny"
"**/.env.*" = "deny"

[permissions.coding.network]
enabled = true

[permissions.coding.network.domains]
"localhost" = "allow"
"127.0.0.1" = "allow"
```

2. Restart Codex with that profile.
3. Request a command that needs an unlisted public domain and explicitly uses:

```json
{
  "sandbox_permissions": "require_escalated",
  "justification": "Run the authorized network command."
}
```

4. Approve the command.
5. Observe that the command still receives the managed-domain allowlist rejection.

Current `main` explains the implementation behavior:

- `sandbox_override_for_first_attempt` selects `EscalatedSandboxWithRestrictions` when denied reads must remain enforced.
- `ToolOrchestrator` keeps `managed_network_active` on that attempt.
- The `ESCALATED_DENY_READ` integration case in `codex-rs/core/tests/suite/network_approval.rs` expects the owner network policy to remain enforced.

### What is the expected behavior?

Do not silently weaken denied-read or owner network policy.

Instead, before asking for approval:

1. State that the requested escalation cannot be fully unsandboxed because denied-read protections must remain active.
2. State that the owner-managed network allowlist will remain active.
3. Identify that approval alone will not grant the requested domain.
4. Point to the supported scoped remedy, such as adding that domain to the active permission profile.
5. Record the effective execution mode as partial/restricted escalation rather than presenting it as ordinary unsandboxed `require_escalated`.

The tool schema and approval UI should not promise “unsandboxed execution” when the selected execution path intentionally preserves restrictions.

### Additional information

Related but distinct reports:

- #49344 covers retained filesystem restrictions and missing diagnostics for browser tests.
- #15309 covers approved escalated commands retaining network restrictions more generally.

This report is specifically about accurately disclosing the combined denied-read plus owner-network behavior that current `main` appears to enforce intentionally.

No credentials, secret values, private repository paths, or device identifiers are included.

issues.title: # zstd request compression: highly compressible content gets a bare 400 instead of the documented 413, and Codex never avoids it

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.167.0

### What subscription do you have?

Pro 500

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6.1-sol

### What platform is your computer?

Linux x86_64（CentOS 8）

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

_No response_

### Codex doctor report

```json

```

### What issue are you seeing?

## Summary

With `features.enable_request_compression` on (the default for ChatGPT auth), Codex zstd-compresses HTTP request
bodies to `chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`. When part of the body decompresses to far more than its compressed
size, the backend answers `400 {"detail":"Bad Request"}`. The same request sent uncompressed succeeds.

The API docs ([production best practices → Compress request bodies](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/production-best-practices))
say the decompressed body must be at most 100× the compressed size, that requests exceeding the limits **return
HTTP 413**, and that 400 is for invalid or incomplete zstd data. A decompression-ratio limit is reasonable; the problems
are:

1. **The Codex backend returns a bare 400, not the documented 413**, so a client can't tell "ratio limit" from corrupted
   data, and the user only sees "Bad Request".
2. **Codex compresses by default and never avoids or recovers from it**: it does not check the ratio before sending and
   does not retry uncompressed. Once a thread's history contains such content, every later turn fails the same way.

**The trigger is local expansion, not the whole-body ratio.** In our sweep below, the image is uniform noise, so every
zstd block compresses about equally and the whole-body ratio is a fair proxy: ≤ ~106× passed, ≥ ~117× failed. With
repeated content, long-distance matches let a single block expand by orders of magnitude while the whole-body ratio
stays low. #60594 reports a 400 at a whole-body ratio of only 2.65×. So the limit is presumably checked per block or per
received piece, not on the whole frame; we have not pinned down the exact rule. An offline model that fails when one
~16 KiB input piece decodes to more than 100× matched most of our captured outcomes, but it misjudged one case near the
boundary. If the check is per received piece, the outcome could also depend on how the body is split in transit. That
might be why a repeated image failed in #60594 but passed for us (2/2); this is speculation.

## Why it matters

- It only happens over HTTP, which Codex uses after falling back from WebSockets. Long conversations with many images
  are the ones that fall back (a reloaded thread resends the whole history in one message), and then **every later
  turn fails** with the same 400, because each turn resends the same history.
- Content that triggers it is ordinary, and nothing needs to be large or modified: a PNG stored without compression, a
  large blank or solid-colour image, or presumably content repeated within the zstd window (the same image twice,
  repetitive logs). A single 4.7 MB image (≈ 6 MB request) is enough. We only tested images.
- The user only sees "Bad Request", with no hint that compression is involved.

## Reproduction

Tested with `codex-cli 0.167.0`, ChatGPT login, Linux x86_64, direct TLS connection to chatgpt.com.

Files (attached below):

- `make_image.py OUT.png P` — a valid 1254×1254 PNG stored without deflate; pixels are noise with probability `P`,
  otherwise one colour. `P` controls the zstd ratio. `P=0` is a solid image.
- `ratio.sh IMAGE` — zstd level-3 ratio of the image's base64 (what the request body mostly is).
- `repro.sh true|false IMAGE` — `codex exec` with one image over plain HTTP (WebSockets off, no retries) and request
  compression on or off.

```sh
python3 make_image.py solid.png 0
./ratio.sh solid.png          # base64 6292308, zstd 2069, ratio 3041.2
./repro.sh true  solid.png    # ERROR: {"detail":"Bad Request"}
./repro.sh false solid.png    # OK
```

### Results

Same image, compression on vs off (3 runs each):

| image | compression on | compression off |
|---|---|---|
| solid.png (ratio ≈ 3041×) | 400 ×3 | OK ×3 |

Compression **on**, varying how well the image compresses (one run each; every image is 4,719,230 bytes, base64
6,292,308 bytes):

| P | zstd ratio of base64 | result |
|---|---|---|
| 0.02 | 28× | OK |
| 0.012 | 45× | OK |
| 0.008 | 64× | OK |
| 0.0055 | 89× | OK |
| 0.005 | 97× | OK |
| 0.0045 | 106× | OK |
| 0.004 | 117× | **400** |
| 0.002 | 205× | **400** |
| 0 | 3041× | **400** |

## Expected

Backend: return the documented **413** (or a specific error message) when a compressed body exceeds the ratio limit,
instead of a bare 400.

Codex client:
- retry once uncompressed when a compressed request gets 413 (or this 400). This works whatever the server's exact
  rule is;
- and/or check the largest per-block expansion of the compressed frame before sending, and send uncompressed when it
  is above ~100×. Whole-body ratio alone is not enough; see the 2.65× case in #60594.

A smaller window (e.g. `window_log` 19) is **not** a general fix. Per the offline analysis in this thread, it removes
long-distance matches (a repeated image) but leaves short repetitions highly expandable: a run of one character still
reaches 32,768× in one block, and this issue's `P=0` solid image 6,241×. Any mitigation should be tested against all
three cases: long-distance repeat, solid image, short repeat.

## Workaround

```toml
[features]
enable_request_compression = false
```

With this, the same requests pass (verified with the images above and with real long conversations that had been
failing every turn).

<details><summary>make_image.py</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Write a valid 1254x1254 RGB PNG whose IDAT is stored without deflate (zlib level 0), so its bytes stay highly
compressible. Each pixel is random noise with probability P, otherwise one solid colour; P sets how well the image
(and its base64 data URL) compresses with zstd. P=0 gives a plain solid-colour image.

Usage: python3 make_image.py OUT.png P [SEED]
"""
import random, struct, sys, zlib

out, p = sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2])
rnd = random.Random(int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 1)
n, solid = 1254, bytes([200, 30, 30])
rows = []
for _ in range(n):
    row = bytearray(b"\x00")  # filter type: none
    for _ in range(n):
        row += bytes(rnd.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(3)) if rnd.random() < p else solid
    rows.append(bytes(row))

def chunk(kind, data):
    return struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + kind + data + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(kind + data) & 0xFFFFFFFF)

png = (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
       + chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", n, n, 8, 2, 0, 0, 0))
       + chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(b"".join(rows), 0))
       + chunk(b"IEND", b""))
open(out, "wb").write(png)
print(out, len(png), "bytes")
```
</details>

<details><summary>repro.sh</summary>

```sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Send one image to the ChatGPT Codex backend over plain HTTP (WebSockets off, no retries) with request compression
# on or off. Usage: ./repro.sh true|false IMAGE.png
set -u
codex exec --skip-git-repo-check --ephemeral \
  -c 'model_provider="chatgpt_http"' \
  -c 'model_providers.chatgpt_http.name="OpenAI"' \
  -c 'model_providers.chatgpt_http.base_url="https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex"' \
  -c 'model_providers.chatgpt_http.wire_api="responses"' \
  -c 'model_providers.chatgpt_http.requires_openai_auth=true' \
  -c 'model_providers.chatgpt_http.supports_websockets=false' \
  -c 'model_providers.chatgpt_http.request_max_retries=0' \
  -c 'model_providers.chatgpt_http.stream_max_retries=0' \
  -c "features.enable_request_compression=$1" \
  "Reply with the single word OK." -i "$2" < /dev/null
```
</details>

<details><summary>ratio.sh</summary>

```sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# zstd ratio of an image's base64 (what the request body mostly is), at Codex's default level 3.
b=$(base64 -w0 "$1" | wc -c); z=$(base64 -w0 "$1" | zstd -3 -q -c | wc -c)
python3 -c "print('$1', 'base64', $b, 'zstd', $z, 'ratio %.1f' % ($b / $z))"
```
</details>

Tested with `codex-cli 0.167.0`, ChatGPT login, Linux x86_64, direct TLS connection to chatgpt.com.

Files (attached below):

- `make_image.py OUT.png P` — a valid 1254×1254 PNG stored without deflate; pixels are noise with probability `P`,
  otherwise one colour. `P` controls the zstd ratio. `P=0` is a solid image.
- `ratio.sh IMAGE` — zstd level-3 ratio of the image's base64 (what the request body mostly is).
- `repro.sh true|false IMAGE` — `codex exec` with one image over plain HTTP (WebSockets off, no retries) and request
  compression on or off.

```sh
python3 make_image.py solid.png 0
./ratio.sh solid.png          # base64 6292308, zstd 2069, ratio 3041.2
./repro.sh true  solid.png    # ERROR: {"detail":"Bad Request"}
./repro.sh false solid.png    # OK
```

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.116.0

### What subscription do you have?

Pro

### Which model were you using?

gpt-5.4 high

### What platform is your computer?

Linux 6.17.0-19-generic x86_64 x86_64

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Ghostty (`TERM=xterm-ghostty`), no tmux, no zellij

### What issue are you seeing?

In an interactive Codex CLI session (the TUI) with Default permissions, a command that requires network access can still fail after I explicitly approve escalation.

The core bug is that the restricted network sandbox policy appears to still be applied to an approved escalated command.

Observed behavior:
- the command is not allowlisted in `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`
- Codex shows an approval prompt for the command
- I approve the prompt
- the command still fails with a GitHub network error instead of running with working host network access

Error from the approved command, e.g. `gh issue`:

```text
error connecting to api.github.com
check your internet connection or https://githubstatus.com
```

This is in the TUI, not exec, app, or app-server, although likely to be reproducible there.

Workarounds:
- add the command prefix to `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`
- or run Codex in full access / dangerous mode so the command bypasses the restricted path entirely

That suggests the approval flow is not fully removing the restricted network policy on the retried command.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start Codex CLI in default permissions mode.
2. Ensure the target network command is not allowlisted in `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`.
3. In an interactive session, ask Codex to run a networked command against a public repo with required escalated permissions, for example:

```bash
gh issue list -R openai/codex --limit 3
```

4. Observe that Codex shows an approval prompt for the command.
5. Approve the prompt.
6. Observe that the command still fails with:

```text
error connecting to api.github.com
check your internet connection or https://githubstatus.com
```

Affected thread id:

- `019d0aa4-3bfe-7100-a9df-9cf93b1d1397`

### What is the expected behavior?

Once the user explicitly approves the escalated command, the retried command should run without the restricted network sandbox policy.

In practice, an approved command that needs network access should be able to reach GitHub successfully instead of still failing with a sandbox-like network error.

### Additional information

This appears related to the broader family of sandbox/network policy propagation issues, but this report is specifically about interactive approval flow:
- the user is prompted
- the user approves
- the retried command still behaves as if restricted network policy is active

Workaround today is to either allowlist the command prefix or run Codex with full access.

### Implementation / fix spec

Probable failure mode:
- the approval flow correctly authorizes a retry without the filesystem sandbox wrapper
- but the retried attempt still inherits the original restricted network policy and/or managed-network enforcement state
- as a result, the command is retried in a partially unrestricted state instead of a truly unrestricted state

Concrete code paths that look involved:
- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs`
  - the escalated retry path builds `SandboxAttempt { sandbox: SandboxType::None, network_policy: turn_ctx.network_sandbox_policy, enforce_managed_network: has_managed_network_requirements, ... }`
  - that means the retry drops the sandbox wrapper but still keeps the original network policy and managed-network flag
- `codex-rs/core/src/sandboxing/mod.rs`
  - `SandboxManager::transform(...)` preserves `network_policy` even when `sandbox == SandboxType::None`
  - if the effective network policy remains restricted, it injects `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1`
  - it also returns an `ExecRequest` that still carries the restricted `network_sandbox_policy`
- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/runtimes/shell/unix_escalation.rs`
  - the shell runtime passes `network_policy` and `enforce_managed_network` into `SandboxTransformRequest`
  - then applies any network/proxy config from the resulting `ExecRequest` to the child environment

Expected implementation behavior:
- when a command is explicitly approved for escalated execution outside the sandbox, the retry should clear both the sandbox wrapper and the restricted network policy for that retry
- the retried execution should not preserve a restricted `NetworkSandboxPolicy` from the original turn if the approved action is intended to run unsandboxed
- the retried execution should not keep managed-network enforcement enabled for that approved unsandboxed retry
- the retried execution should not inject or preserve `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1` for that retry
- proxy/env rewriting that is only appropriate for the restricted sandbox path should not remain active on the approved unsandboxed retry

Suggested implementation points:
- audit the retry path in `codex-rs/core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs` where an approved command is rerun after a sandbox/network denial
- make the approved retry derive both sandbox mode and effective network policy from the escalation decision, not only sandbox mode
- update the transform/execution path in `codex-rs/core/src/sandboxing/mod.rs` so an approved unsandboxed retry cannot silently carry forward a restricted network policy
- verify the shell execution path in `codex-rs/core/src/tools/runtimes/shell/unix_escalation.rs` does not reapply restricted-network env/proxy behavior on an approved unsandboxed retry
- add regression coverage for interactive approval flow, not only allowlisted/trusted execpolicy flow

Acceptance criteria:
- in a default-permissions interactive CLI session, a non-allowlisted networked command that triggers approval succeeds after the user approves escalation
- the retried command does not see `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1` and can resolve and connect to network
- - behavior for commands that remain sandboxed is unchanged
- existing allowlisted/trusted-command behavior and child/subagent behavior are not regressed

issues.title: [ChatGPT Web][Sep 2026 UI] Conversation workflow regressions: native links/new-tab behavior removed and direct Delete action lost

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
### Summary

The recent ChatGPT web UI update introduced several related conversation-navigation and lifecycle regressions on `chatgpt.com`.

These are not requests for new advanced features. They are previously available browser/UI workflows that disappeared with the new interface.

The regressions I can reproduce are:

1. **“New chat” no longer behaves like a normal browser link.**
2. **Existing conversation entries no longer behave like normal browser links.**
3. As a consequence, standard browser actions are lost:
   - Right-click → **Open link in new tab**
   - **Ctrl+Click**
   - **Middle-click**
   - **Copy link address**
4. **Delete has been removed from the menu of the currently open conversation**, forcing the user to find the same conversation again in the sidebar/search before it can be deleted.

These changes all move conversation management away from direct/native browser interaction and toward extra sidebar/search navigation.

### Environment

- Surface: `chatgpt.com`
- OS: Windows 11
- Browser: Microsoft Edge
- First observed: immediately after the September 25, 2026 ChatGPT web UI update
- Reproduced again on September 27, 2026

### Regression 1 — New chat can no longer be opened directly in a new tab

Previously, “New chat” behaved like a link.

Expected browser workflows included:

- Right-click → Open link in new tab
- Ctrl+Click
- Middle-click

With the current UI, right-clicking “New chat” produces the generic page context menu rather than a link context menu.

This means a user who wants to preserve the current conversation and start another one in parallel now has to:

```
open another browser tab
→ navigate to ChatGPT
→ start a new chat there
```

instead of simply opening “New chat” in another tab.

### Regression 2 — Existing conversations no longer preserve native link behavior

The same problem affects conversation entries.

When conversation entries are not real links, standard browser navigation is lost:

- no native Open in new tab
- no Ctrl+Click
- no middle-click
- no Copy link address

This is especially disruptive for workflows where several conversations are used in parallel and compared against each other.

### Regression 3 — Browser-native context-menu functionality has been removed

The practical issue is not only the absence of an explicit “Open in new tab” button.

The new UI removes normal browser link semantics entirely.

That means the browser can no longer provide functionality it already knows how to provide for free.

This is a regression from normal web behavior and makes ChatGPT navigation less interoperable with the browser.

### Regression 4 — Delete is no longer available from the currently open conversation

Before the UI update, the menu of the currently open conversation included **Delete**.

The previous workflow was:

```
open chat
→ use chat
→ decide whether it is worth keeping
→ delete it immediately from the currently open conversation
```

The current workflow is:

```
open chat
→ use chat
→ decide it is not worth keeping
→ leave the current context
→ find the same chat again in the sidebar or search
→ open another menu
→ delete it there
```

During the rollout I also observed inconsistent behavior inside the same account: an older existing chat still exposed the direct Delete action while a chat using the current UI did not.

Temporary Chat is not an equivalent workaround because the user often does not know at the beginning of a conversation whether the conversation will be worth keeping.

### Why these regressions matter together

These changes all increase navigation and context-switching overhead.

For intensive technical/development use, parallel ChatGPT tabs are not cosmetic. They are used to:

- preserve one conversation while starting another task;
- compare outputs between conversations;
- inspect previous project context;
- supervise coding/agent work in parallel;
- keep long-running technical threads available without repeatedly searching for them.

The removal of native link behavior forces additional navigation every time a parallel conversation is needed.

The removal of direct Delete forces the user to search for a conversation that is already open in front of them.

This also discourages cleanup: chats remain in history not because the user wants to keep them, but because deleting them now requires extra search/navigation work.

### Cost / supervision impact

For coding-heavy use, model and agent usage is metered and valuable enough that users cannot simply ignore efficiency, leave everything running indefinitely, and rerun work whenever something goes wrong.

Active human supervision, context preservation, and comparison between threads are part of the real cost of using the product.

A UI change that repeatedly adds navigation, searching, and context switching therefore increases the human supervision cost of the product even if each individual interaction only adds a few seconds.

Repeated across a development day, that becomes significant.

### Steps to reproduce

#### Native-link / new-tab regression

1. Open `https://chatgpt.com/` in Microsoft Edge on Windows 11.
2. Right-click **New chat** in the sidebar.
3. Observe that the browser shows the generic page context menu rather than a link context menu.
4. Try Ctrl+Click or middle-click on **New chat**.
5. Observe that it does not provide the previous native new-tab workflow.
6. Repeat with an existing conversation entry.

#### Direct Delete regression

1. Open a normal ChatGPT conversation.
2. Open the three-dot menu for the currently open conversation.
3. Observe that **Delete** is not available there in the current UI.
4. To delete the conversation, go to the sidebar/search.
5. Find the same conversation again.
6. Open its sidebar menu.
7. Delete it there.

### Expected behavior

ChatGPT should preserve standard browser navigation semantics.

Preferred behavior:

- “New chat” is a real link/deep link where technically possible.
- Conversation entries are real links/deep links.
- Right-click, Ctrl+Click, and middle-click work normally.
- Copy link address is available.
- The currently open conversation includes a direct Delete action with the existing confirmation dialog.

If ChatGPT requires custom JavaScript navigation internally, an equivalent explicit **Open in new tab** action should be provided without removing native browser behavior where possible.

### Actual behavior

The current UI replaces direct/native workflows with additional in-app navigation:

- New chat cannot be opened in another tab using normal browser link behavior.
- Existing conversation entries lose native link actions.
- Standard right-click/Ctrl+Click/middle-click workflows are removed.
- Deleting the currently open conversation requires finding the conversation again in the sidebar/search.

### Scope

I am grouping these together because they appeared with the same recent web UI change and they have the same user-facing effect: conversation navigation and lifecycle management now require more in-app searching and context switching.

If these are owned by different internal components, please split them internally as needed, but they represent one coherent workflow regression from the user side.

### Related community reports

Similar regressions are already being discussed in the OpenAI Developer Community, including reports about:

- conversations no longer being normal links;
- middle-click / Ctrl+Click no longer opening chats in new tabs;
- “New chat” losing new-tab behavior;
- recent ChatGPT web UI regressions affecting established workflows.

The important point here is that this is not a request to invent a new workflow. It is a request to restore standard browser and conversation-management behavior that previously existed.

issues.title: codex cloud does not discover current Cloud environments

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
# codex cloud does not discover current Cloud environments

## What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.160.0`, the npm latest release at the time of this check.

## Authentication

ChatGPT authentication. The CLI and desktop app use the same account. Token refresh succeeds. No API key is in use.

## Platform

macOS, `Darwin 24.6.0 arm64 arm`. I ran these checks through a terminal PTY.

## What issue are you seeing?

I can see two owned, Private environments in Settings > Codex Cloud. Neither has an Unpublished badge. The settings catalog returns both environments with current versions when requested with `scope=user&omitDraft=true`; it returns no further page. The workspace catalog returns zero environments. Legacy Codex Cloud shows “No cloud environments yet”.

On the same account, `codex cloud` shows only “All Environments (Global)” in its environment picker. I get the same result from a checkout with a GitHub remote and from `/tmp`.

An explicit submission exits 1 with:

```text
Error: no cloud environments are available for this workspace
```

The CLI's catalog requests return HTTP 200. Its repository-specific lookup returns zero environments. `codex cloud list --json` returns `{"tasks":[],"cursor":null}`; I understand that this is an execution-task list, not an environment inventory.

## What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use a ChatGPT account with current Cloud environments visible in Settings > Codex Cloud and no environments in Legacy Codex Cloud.
2. Authenticate the latest CLI with that account.
3. Run `codex cloud`, open the environment picker, and inspect the choices without submitting.
4. Compare the picker from the repository checkout and from `/tmp`.
5. Try `codex cloud exec --env '<environment identifier>' --branch main --attempts 1 'Read-only environment canary; report pwd and git HEAD, then stop.'`.

The submission above fails during environment resolution before creating a task. No canary has run.

## What is the expected behavior?

The CLI should list accessible current Cloud environments and accept the supported identifier for fresh task dispatch. If this environment type requires a different CLI route, please document the command and identifier mapping.

The [CLI documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands#codex-cloud) describes task submission through `codex cloud exec --env`, and the [Cloud overview](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud) describes starting Cloud work from the CLI.

## Diagnostic evidence

- Current settings load `/api/codex-cloud/v1/environment-configs?scope=user&limit=100&omitDraft=true`. Its entries use `provider=caas`, stable IDs with an `asenvcfg_` component, and version IDs with a `cecfgver_` component.
- CLI 0.160.0's [environment discovery code](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/env_detect.rs) queries `/backend-api/wham/environments/by-repo/github/OWNER/REPO` and `/backend-api/wham/environments`.
- Its [resolve_environment_id function](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/lib.rs#L203) rejects an empty catalog before matching `--env`. Replacing a version ID with a stable ID therefore cannot bypass this result.
- I compared `env_detect.rs` in 0.160.0 and 0.162.0-alpha.3; the bytes match. I did not install or run the alpha release.
- `CODEX_CLOUD_TASKS_BASE_URL`, `CODEX_CLOUD_TASKS_MODE` and `CODEX_STARTING_DIFF` are unset.
- The existing doctor run passed installation/version, authentication, HTTP connectivity and the Responses WebSocket handshake. It also reported optional local MCP/state/terminal warnings; I have no evidence that they affect catalog discovery.

These observations suggest a mismatch between the current and legacy catalogs. Please confirm whether the released CLI supports the current environments and identify the supported repair or route.

Related: [#49966](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49966) reports the new/legacy selection difference in the web UI. This report supplies CLI discovery and resolution evidence. [#15544](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/15544) concerns empty task-list reporting and was closed as not planned; this request concerns access to environments that exist in the current catalog.

I omitted account identifiers, environment identifiers, repository names, credentials and raw local logs.
