issues.body:
**What is measured here, and how it differs from the existing reports:** the provider request array diverges from the
previous request on the **first** request of a large share of turns (25-38% of stored user messages, measured over a
full local day on two independent deployments), not on every request as #182891 reports. #182891 and #198373 are on
OpenAI-compatible routes; the evidence below includes an Anthropic-compatible route. #99495 (closed) describes two
other append-only violations on the Anthropic route; the mechanism reported here is a rewritten *history* entry on
the first request of a turn, with the provider-visible request metadata identical on both sides.

**Related:** #182891 (open, same symptom on an OpenAI-compatible route, reported as happening on every request — this report measures it at request=1 in 25-38% of turns), #198373 (open, history rewritten between turns on an OpenAI-compatible route), #99495 (closed, two append-only violations on the Anthropic route), #143242 (closed, runtime-only event turns).

**Measured:** 2026-11-13, two independent deployments, OpenClaw 2026.11.3 (847611d), node 24.22.1.

#### Observation

Prompt-cache reads are dropped on `historyRewrite` at the **first request of a large share of stored user messages** — 25% on deployment 1, 38% on deployment 2. An earlier report of this report said "nearly every turn"; that is withdrawn. The detector reports the first index at which the request array differs from the previous request's array. A divergence at index N invalidates the cached prefix from N onward, whether the cause is a rewritten message at N or a shift of the whole array from N.

How the index is computed (`dist/attempt-system-prompt-prepare-*.mjs`, ~line 745):

```js
const history = params.messages.map((message, index) => fingerprintMessage(message, previous?.history[index]));
const divergence = previous ? previous.history.findIndex((message, index) => message !== history[index]) : -1;
```

This is a positional comparison, not an identity match. `message N` therefore means "the first position at which the arrays differ" — it does **not** by itself distinguish a rewritten message from an inserted or removed one. The log line carries no message count, so the two cannot be separated from the log alone (see open instrumentation request).

Per-deployment, window = local day 2026-11-13, source = `journalctl --user -u openclaw-gateway` lines matching `cache read dropped <n> -> <n>`:

| deployment | drops | lost cacheRead tokens | controllable share | content-level share | positions seen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A (deployment 1, full local day) | 214 | 17,107,601 | 79.0% | 124/214 = 58% | 0 … 313 |
| B (deployment 2, full local day) | 184 | 12,691,590 | 88.8% | 144/184 = 78.3% | 0 … 177 |

Counting rule: a drop event is a journal line matching `cache read dropped <n> -> <n>`. On deployment 1 the loose
phrase match and the strict pattern agree exactly - 30 days: 389 = 389, 2026-11-13: 214 = 214 - so that
denominator has no phantom line. On deployment 2 the loose match returns one extra line (185 against 184): a
`[tools] dispatch_action failed` payload that quotes the phrase inside an embedded instruction. The lost-token
total (12,691,590) and the fragment count (144) are unaffected; only the denominator moves. Every one of the
214 lines on deployment 1 also receives a class token, one of them "unattributed".


Total lost cacheRead on deployment 1 over the day: **17.1 million tokens**. Tokens per class, deployment 1: `historyRewrite` 97 lines / 6,339,840, `compaction` 34 / 4,660,884, `provider-cache-reuse-lost` 45 / 2,529,024, `systemPrompt` 18 / 1,898,112, `systemPromptSuffix` 12 / 1,027,397, `runtimeContextCarrier` 5 / 301,624, `tools` 2 / 251,904, `unattributed` 1 / 98,816.

Denominator, so the frequency is checkable: deployment 1 has 488 user messages stored today against 124 divergences = **25%**; deployment 2 has 376 user messages against 144 divergences = **38%**. Not "every turn" — "between a quarter and two fifths of stored user messages".

Excluded from "controllable": `provider-cache-reuse-lost:unchanged-prefix`, which is not caused by us. Measured on deployment 1: n=42, median gap since previous call 9.2 s, max 27 s, 0 of 42 above 60 s — identical bytes failing to hit cache seconds apart, consistent with provider-side replica routing, not TTL.

#### Cost is not the index

The divergence index is a fingerprint artefact, not a measure of the damage: no cached share can be derived from this line, because `promptTokens` is not the provider's total. Measured in absolute tokens instead (deployment 1, historyRewrite n=119, window to 21:52):

- dropped `cacheRead`: median **73,472**, p10 6,144, p90 130,048
- `cacheRead` after the drop: median **33,280**, p10 4,864
- dropped ÷ previous `cacheRead`: median **68.8%**

All 208 drop events up to 21:52: median drop 81,664, after median 31,232. Over the full local day there are 214 drop lines and 124 positioned `historyRewrite` events; the token medians above are the 21:52 subset and are labelled as such.

So it is neither a full prefix rebuild nor a small correction: the median event loses about two thirds of the cached prefix and keeps a third. deployment 2 reports the same shape (historyRewrite n=144: median drop 71,680, 66.8% of previous `cacheRead`, after median 38,848).

**A ratio against `promptTokens` must not be published.** On deployment 1, **86 of 208 events up to 21:52 (41%) have `cacheRead` above `promptTokens` before the drop**, and deployment 2 reports 71 of 172 (41.3%) — so `promptTokens` is not the provider's total input and any "percent cached" computed from it is meaningless. An earlier version of this report quoted such percentages; they are withdrawn.

#### Three mechanisms, separated by the byte delta already in the log

Each drop line carries `requests={"previous":{"requestBytes":N,…},"current":{…}}`. The delta separates the mechanisms without new instrumentation. deployment 1, n=109 historyRewrite events with both byte values (full day):

| position | grow | shrink | median delta | reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ≥20 | 40 | 3 | +10,940 B | one user message added at the tail — the injection |
| 1–19 | 7 | 25 | −78,443 B | messages removed at that index — window rebuild |
| 0 | 11 | 23 | −6,461 B | head replaced — LCM compaction (see below) |

deployment 2 reports the same shape in its own byte sample (n=115, band **1–19** as deployment 2 corrected it after an off-by-one of mine: 29 of 31 shrink, median −76,021 B; ≥20: 50 of 53 grow, median +17,289 B; index 0: 18 shrink / 13 grow, median −11,781 B), so the carrier alone is never the whole delta on either deployment. deployment 2's byte figures come from its own full day (115 of its 144 fragments carry both byte values) and must not be summed with the numbers above.

Index 0 in a large session coincides with summarisation, which never logs as `compaction`: **28 of deployment 1's 34 index-0 events fall within 5 minutes of a `summaries` row in `lcm.db` (20 leaf, 8 condensed).** In a small session (one user message), index 0 is simply the only candidate position the positional comparison can reach, so injection and growth coincide there.

That association is weaker than it first looked. Against a null model over the same day, both classes sit far closer to a summary than chance — and on deployment 1 the index-0 class is **not** tighter than the rest:

| deployment 1 | n | median distance | above 300 s |
|---|---|---|---|
| index 0 | 36 | 63 s | 6/36 (17%) |
| index >0 | 85 | 98 s | 14/85 (16%) |
| random | 400 | 306 s | 201/400 (50%) |

deployment 2 does show the separation (index 0: median 35 s, 0/38 above 300 s; index >0: median 76 s, 22/101 above 300 s). So "the head is replaced by a leaf summary" is a hypothesis that holds on deployment 2 and does not replicate on deployment 1 — and the journal's `compaction` class undercounts summarisation by roughly 50×, which is why the head event was invisible in the first place.

Reproduction without a debug build: pick a session with exactly one event per turn and read the index sequence. deployment 2 example `9a626a3f`: index 6 then 7, one higher per turn. deployment 2 `68464933`: 5↓ 45↑ 6↓ 62↑ 84↑ 85↑ — both mechanisms alternating in one session.

#### Field-level evidence

deployment 1, historyRewrite n=124 (full local day): divergence at index 0 = **36** (33 user, 3 assistant); index > 0 = **88** (83 user, 5 assistant).

deployment 2, historyRewrite n=144: **144/144 at role `user`**, positions 0–177.

Field signatures on the drop lines (literal):
- `content` alone, or `content + envelope.__openclaw`: dominant on both deployments.
- `content.length, content[0].type, content[0].id/name/arguments, content[0].thinking, content[0].thinkingSignature`: **8 events, deployment 1 only**. These are assistant messages carrying tool calls — a user message has no `arguments` or `thinkingSignature`, so this is an assistant message whose fingerprint changed after it was sent (write-back).
- `envelope.runtimeContext, envelope.runtimeContextCarrier`: **1 event on deployment 1, 0 of 144 on deployment 2.** The carrier field is present in the code path but is not the dominant driver.

Cross-deployment differences are stated as such and not averaged: write-back 8 vs 0; carrier field 1 vs 0; role split 116 user / 8 assistant vs 144 user / 0 assistant.

#### Where it happens

deployment 1, full day, per class and per request index (sums to 214; 164 at `request=1`, 20 at 2–3, 30 at 4+):

| class | request=1 | request=2–3 | request=4+ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `historyRewrite` (97) | 97 | 0 | 0 |
| `compaction` (34) | 34 | 0 | 0 |
| `systemPrompt` (18) | 18 | 0 | 0 |
| `systemPromptSuffix` (12) | 12 | 0 | 0 |
| `tools` (2) | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| `runtimeContextCarrier` (5) | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| `provider-cache-reuse-lost` (45) | 0 | 18 | 27 |
| `unattributed` (1) | 0 | 0 | 1 |

So the two phenomena separate cleanly by request index: our own rewrites occur once per turn, at the boundary; `unchanged-prefix` never occurs on the first call and is a mid-turn provider miss on identical bytes.

#### What is established

1. The injected runtime-context block is **never persisted on user messages**. deployment 1: 0 of 37,989 stored messages carry it on `role=user` (2 hits are `role=tool`, echoes of our own command output). deployment 2: 0 of 44,040 (3 apparent user hits are Discord attachments quoting the text).
2. `hasRuntimeContextMarker(message)` tests a **field**, not text: `message.role === "user" && (message.runtimeContext !== undefined || message.runtimeContextCarrier === true)` (`dist/types-*.mjs`).
3. The transcript store has **no column** for that field (`messages`: message_id, conversation_id, seq, role, content, token_count, created_at, identity_hash, openclaw_sender_metadata, large_content, transcript_entry_id, stable_event_key). A carrier therefore cannot come **out of** storage — which does not exclude a carrier being set **on** an existing message in the assembled array at request time.

#### Candidates — none proven

- **C1 — injected-but-not-persisted runtime context.** A message is sent *with* a block and stored *without* it; on the next turn the same position is rebuilt clean, so `content` differs from what the previous request contained. This produces a trail of "vanished injections" rather than one culprit position. Two sub-variants, both consistent with the data: the block is **appended** as a separate message, or the carrier field is set **synthetically on an existing user message** at assembly time. Which of the two applies determines *where* the damage lands: append keeps it at the tail, a synthetic carrier on the first user message of the window puts it at position 0 — and after a compaction the "first of the window" moves, which matches the spread positions (5, 48, 74, 110) as well as the concentration on position 0.
- **C2 — assistant `usage` write-back.** `usage`, `model`, `provider`, `api` changing on assistant messages after the fact (10–12% of events).
- **C3 — volatile envelope fields** (`timestamp`, `idempotencyKey`, `__openclaw`), 7–14% of events.

Explicitly **not** claimed as cause: `prependRuntimeContextForModel`. Its carrier branch (`messages.findIndex(hasRuntimeContextMarker)` + `messages.with(...)`) is reachable only if a carrier exists in the assembled array; whether one does is exactly the open question. What is ruled out is that the carrier comes from persistent storage.

Also unresolved: whether a divergence at index N is a rewritten message at N or a shifted array from N. The log line carries the index but not the message count, so both readings survive. Logging `messages.length` next to the index would settle it in one line — that is a separate request, and only useful together with the index.

#### Design rule (proposed fix direction)

Whatever is injected into a message must either be persisted with it, or not be sent once that message is history. Today's combination — injected at send time, absent from storage — is by construction one cache miss per turn.

#### Open question for the maintainer

Which of the three candidates writes the bytes? A request-side capture of position N across two consecutive requests settles it. `OPENCLAW_PROMPT_CACHE_ASSERT=1` turns the warning into a throw that names the message index and changed fields, which is enough to identify the first diverging position without dumping prompt content.

#### Related measurement, kept separate

Booked prompts reached 330,513 tokens (deployment 1) and 299,976 (deployment 2) while `maxAssemblyTokenBudget` was 150,000 — raised to 400,000 at 20:47 local, so these are pre-change numbers — against a median of 106k. The ledger contains no identifiable summarizer traffic, so whether those calls are main-lane or compaction is unresolved; it is not part of this issue.

#### Corrected classification of `providerPrefix` (one population; deployment 1)

Single parse of deployment 1 over the full local day 2026-11-13 00:00 -> 2026-11-14 00:00: 124 positioned `historyRewrite` events, out of 124 `historyRewrite` lines and 214 `cache read dropped` lines.

| `providerPrefix` | n | share |
|---|---|---|
| `message:N.content` (content-only change) | 55 | 44% |
| `message:N` (whole message object) | 34 | 27% |
| multi-field (role+content+tool_calls+other) | 18 | 15% |
| `unavailable` | 15 | 12% |
| two odd forms (`tools`, `message:54,parameters:stream_options`) | 2 | 2% |

Same population, split by position and by role:

| band | events | user | assistant | content-only | whole-object | multi-field | unavailable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| index 0 | 36 | 33 | 3 | 32 | 0 | 2 | 2 |
| 1-19 | 39 | 34 | 5 | 17 | 0 | 15 | 7 |
| 20+ | 49 | 49 | 0 | 6 | 34 | 1 | 6 |

Reading: index 0 = 32/36 content-only (89%); positions 1-19 = 17/39 (44%) with 15 of the 18 multi-field events; positions 20+ = 6/49 content-only (12%) and 34/49 whole-object (69%). Role split over the whole population: 116 user / 8 assistant, the assistant events being the write-back ones. All 124 of 124 sit at request=1.

deployment 2, for comparison (its own population, not averaged): index 0 = 30/31 (97%), 1-19 = 19/31 (61%), 20+ = 6/51 (12%) content-only with 45/51 (88%) whole-message. Both deployments are content-majority at the head; the whole-object share at the tail is what differs. **Only the content-only column is comparable across deployments**: deployment 1 has 124 events, deployment 2 144 of which 30 carry no prefix, so the whole-object column must not be read across deployments.

Withdrawn from earlier versions of this report: the claim that the two deployments mirror each other (it rested on a coarse bucket), a count of 51 message-level events where the bucket was 67 (51 + 15 + 1), and per-position buckets taken from a different sample than the role split. The table above is one population and is the only one to use. Not a limitation of this measurement but of the field itself: **30 of deployment 2's 144 events carry no `providerPrefix` at all**, which is why the share is stated on two denominators (144 and 114) and why the prefix-form comparison between deployments rests on the content-only column alone.

Class token and rewrite fragment are **two axes on the same line**, and on deployment 1 they do not coincide. The class token sums exactly to the line count; the fragment says a positional comparison found a differing message. A share of "historyRewrite" is therefore a **class** share, and it is deployment- and window-dependent (deployment 1 97 of 214 = 45%, deployment 2 127 of 184 = 69%). The quantity that is defined identically on both deployments is the **fragment**: the event where a message sent to the provider no longer matches the one sent on the previous request. That is 124 of 214 on deployment 1 and 144 of 184 on deployment 2, and every one of those events sits at `request=1` on both.

The class breakdown on deployment 1 over the full day: `historyRewrite` 97, `provider-cache-reuse-lost` 45, `compaction` 34, `systemPrompt` 18, `systemPromptSuffix` 12, `runtimeContextCarrier` 5, `tools` 2, `unattributed` 1 — summing to 214 exactly. Of the 124 fragments, **97 are classed `historyRewrite` and 27 as a system-prompt break** (16 `systemPrompt`, 11 `systemPromptSuffix`).

**The split is real on both deployments; only its magnitude is deployment-specific.** deployment 2, measured with the same method over its own full day (184 drop events), shows the same split, smaller: **13 of its 144 fragments (9%) also carry a system-prompt marker** (11 `systemPromptSuffix` + 2 `systemPrompt`), against 27 of 124 (22%) on deployment 1. This is an overlap count, not a partition: all 144 fragments are `historyRewrite` by the fragment axis, and a line can carry several labels. Re-measured with the strict counting rule on deployment 2 over its own full day: **184 drop events** (a journal line matching `cache read dropped <n> -> <n>`), **144 fragments**, every one of them `role=user` and at `request=1`, at positions 0-177, for 12,691,590 lost tokens. Classified by the first label after `via <route>;`: `historyRewrite` 127 lines (127 of them with a fragment), `systemPromptSuffix` 11 (11), `systemPrompt` 2 (2), `runtimeContextCarrier` 21 (4), `compaction` 3 (0), `provider-cache-reuse-lost` 20 (0) - so the fragment column splits as 127 + 11 + 2 + 4 = 144. The four fragments carried by `runtimeContextCarrier` lines sit on the Anthropic-messages route, where `providerPrefix=unavailable` (no byte pair exists), at positions 48, 65, 32 and 108; three of the four change only `envelope.timestamp`. A looser phrase match returns 185 lines on deployment 2, because one extra line is a tool-error payload that quotes the phrase inside an embedded instruction instead of reporting a drop; 184 is therefore the denominator, and the lost-token total and the fragment count are unaffected by that difference. Two readings are open and neither is proven: (a) deployment 1's system prompt changed during the day — a config, steering or tooling change, which is a different mechanism with a different fix (do not edit settings mid-session), or (b) a route difference between the two deployments. Until one of them is excluded, the *cause* is attributable to deployment 1 only; the *phenomenon* — a system-prompt break coinciding with a divergence — is present on both deployments.

What the 30 system-prompt lines on deployment 1 look like in time and content, since "the operator changed a setting" is the obvious alternative explanation and had to be tested rather than assumed:

- They are **spread over fifteen different hours** (01, 02, 03, 06, 07, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20, 23 — 30 lines total, 2 to 5 per hour at most). There is **no burst at any configuration edit**: deployment 1's `openclaw.json` was written at 03:24–03:33, 10:34, 13:36, 14:00, 19:05 and 20:40–20:52 that day, and no minute-level cluster follows any of those writes.
- The digest that changed is dominated by the catch-all section: `Other` 27, `Tooling` 8, `Skills` 2, `Runtime` 2 (a line can name several). A settings edit that changes the skills or tool list would show up as `Skills`/`Tooling`, not as `Other`.

So the edits happened, and they cannot be excluded in principle, but their timing does not explain the distribution. The mechanism stays open; the only deployment-1-specific candidate measured so far is the exec-tool availability flag (`processToolAvailabilityRef`), which invalidated the prompt cache on deployment 1 and not on deployment 2 over an earlier 48-hour window, with the trigger still unproven.

Class by request index, deployment 1: every class except the two provider-side ones occurs at `request=1` without exception (164 of 214 events), `provider-cache-reuse-lost` never does (0 of 45), and `runtimeContextCarrier` sits mostly inside the turn (1 of 5 at `request=1`).

#### Cross-deployment additions (a second, independent deployment, 2026-11-14)

Three additions that were agreed between the deployments and belong in the report rather than in a footnote.

1. **Only the content-only share is comparable across deployments.** deployment 1 has 124 positioned events; deployment 2
   has 144, of which 30 carry no `providerPrefix` at all. The whole-object column must not be read across
   deployments without that disclaimer, and the share is therefore stated on two denominators (144 and 114).
2. **Class and fragment are two different axes on the same log line.** The 214 deployment 1 drops carry a class
   token that sums exactly to 214 (97 / 45 / 34 / 18 / 12 / 5 / 2 / 1). Of the 124 message-divergence
   fragments, 97 are classed `historyRewrite` and **27 are a system-prompt break** (16 `systemPrompt`,
   11 `systemPromptSuffix`). Those 27 are not message rewrites; a report that counts every fragment as a
   message rewrite overstates that mechanism by roughly a quarter. The same split exists on deployment 2,
   smaller: 13 of its 144 fragments (2 `systemPrompt` + 11 `systemPromptSuffix`), i.e. 9% against 22% on
   deployment 1. The phenomenon is therefore cross-deployment and the magnitude is deployment-specific.
3. **The class distribution is deployment- and window-dependent; the fragment is not.** "historyRewrite is
   79–85% of drops" holds for deployment 2 (144 of 184) and not for deployment 1 (97 of 214 = 45%). The stable
   quantity is the fragment: 124 of 214 on deployment 1 and 144 of 184 on deployment 2 are lines where a sent message
   no longer matches the previous request.
4. **The provider-visible request metadata does not change between the two requests.** For every
   fragment where both requests are logged in full (115 of 144 on deployment 2), the metadata is identical on
   the previous and the current request: `modelHash`, `routeHash`, `cacheKeyHash`, `prefixHash`,
   `cacheKeyPresent` and `previousResponseIdPresent` are equal in 115 of 115, `serviceTier` is equal in
   60 of 60 where the field is present, and `prefixBytes` is 4096 on both sides in all 230 entries.
   Only the message content diverges. The divergence therefore cannot be attributed to a changed
   model, route, tier or cache key. Intent is not observable and is not claimed.
5. **Talk realtime is not in play here.** On deployment 2 the journal for 2026-11-13 contains zero lines
   matching `talk-realtime`, `realtime-consult` or `talk realtime`, and the config has no talk realtime
   key. The mechanism of #179236 (Talk realtime consults rewriting history, closed 2026-11-11) is
   therefore not the cause of these drops: same symptom, different cause.

issues.body:
## Summary
When a parent session yields while awaiting child subagent runs, a later revocation of the requester operator authority makes the child completion delivery fail permanently. The parent never receives the completion and stays in a waiting state. The failure is reported with a constant error string that does not say why the authority was revoked, so the failure cannot be attributed from logs.

## Environment
openclaw 2026.9.8, shipped bundle (dist).

## Where (verified against the shipped bundle)
File: dist/session-followup-completion-<hash>.mjs

- :174  async function withRequesterCronAuthority(params, run)
- :183  if (authority.operatorAuthority) throw new Error("Requester operator authority is no longer current");
- :195, :200  if (!current()) throw new Error("Requester operator authority is no longer current");

The same module contains the currency check isCurrent(authority), which returns false when:
- the operator authority is no longer current;
- authority.lifecycleGeneration !== getAgentRunLifecycleGeneration();
- the session authority set no longer contains this authority.

The module also exports revokeRequesterCronAuthority / revokeRequesterCronAuthorityBatch, i.e. revocation is an explicit, supported path.

## Observed behaviour
- A child run ends cleanly (status: done, execution: finished) while its recorded delivery status is failed, with failure text referencing the error above.
- The parent session that was awaiting children never wakes; no completion event arrives; the interface remains in a waiting-for-subtasks state indefinitely.
- The child result is not lost: it can still be read back from the child session.

## Gaps
1. The thrown Error carries only the constant message. No reason code, no cause detail, nothing that identifies which currency condition failed or which code path revoked the authority.
2. Because of (1), a failed delivery cannot be traced from logs alone; identifying the cause required reading the bundle source.

## Impact
- Parent-side waits can hang indefinitely with no signal to the requester.
- Automated flows that depend on yield/completion handoff stall silently.
- Self-diagnosis is not possible for operators.

## Requests
1. Include a machine-readable reason (and, where safe, a short cause detail) in the thrown error and in the recorded delivery failure.
2. Provide a recoverable or at least observable failure path (for example a delivery-failure event the requester can observe and re-attach to), instead of leaving the wait unresolved.
3. Document which actions revoke a pending requester authority.

## Reproduction caveat
We could not build a deterministic minimal reproduction, because the revocation path is not logged. The above is based on the shipped bundle source plus observed behaviour. We are happy to test a build that logs the revocation reason.

issues.body:
### Summary
In browser realtime Talk (`talk.realtime.mode: "realtime"`, OpenAI WebRTC, `brain: "agent-consult"`), everything the user says while an agent consult is running is stored and shown as one merged user bubble, and the assistant's spoken replies for that stretch as one merged assistant bubble. Please keep one bubble per finalized utterance, as split mode (`stt-tts`) already does.

### Problem to solve
- With `mode: "stt-tts"`, every utterance becomes its own chat turn and its own bubble. The transcript is easy to read, but every reply waits for a full agent turn (typically 15–25 s with a large model).
- With `mode: "realtime"` (`consultRouting: "provider-direct"`), the conversation is fast, but every user utterance spoken while a consult is in flight lands in a single user message. The provider's direct replies and the consult answer for that stretch land in a single assistant message.
- In practice, a two-minute voice exchange reads as two long walls of text: all user speech in one bubble, all replies in another. It is hard to see who said what, when, and in response to what.

Users are forced to choose between a readable transcript and a usable response time.

### Proposed solution
Persist and render each finalized realtime transcript as its own message, in arrival order, also while a consult is in flight. `handleTranscript` already assigns a separate `entryId` per final transcript, so the separation already exists at the source. The merge seems to happen when entries are committed and rendered per consult round.

If strict per-utterance persistence conflicts with consult input adoption (realtime-sessions.md: "Speech finalized while an accepted consult is starting remains visible in history…"), an alternative would be to keep the adoption semantics but render separate bubbles in the Control UI, grouped visually by round.

### Alternatives considered
- `stt-tts`: separate bubbles, but too slow for conversation.
- Pausing until each reply finishes: reduces merging, but is unnatural in a live conversation.
- Lower thinking or a faster model for consults (`consultThinkingLevel`, `consultFastMode`): shortens the merge window but does not remove it.

### Impact
Affects anyone using browser realtime Talk with agent consults. Readability of the saved conversation is the main cost. No data is lost: all utterances are in history, just merged.

### Evidence/examples
- OpenClaw 2026.11.2, Control UI in the browser, OpenAI realtime WebRTC, `brain: "agent-consult"`, `consultRouting: "provider-direct"`.
- Session history shows one user and one assistant message per consult round, e.g. a user message containing several separate spoken sentences (with transcription noise tags such as `[breath]`, `[click]`) committed at the same second as the assistant message for that round.
- Related but distinct issues: #184263, #197432, #164531.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?
No.

issues.body:
# Issue draft — memory status --json hides disabled agents behind an empty array

## Summary

With memory search disabled (`memory.search.enabled: false`), `openclaw memory status --json` returns `[]` — disabled agents are silently missing from the documented machine-readable aggregate. The same CLI family's search path already emits a proper disabled document (`{agentId, status: "disabled"}`), so the two disagree, and scripts cannot distinguish "no agents" from "all agents disabled".

## Real-CLI evidence (source checkout of main `1c0ca3120c5`, isolated HOME/state/config)

With `{"agents":{"defaults":{"workspace": ...}}, "memory": {"search": {"enabled": false}}}`:

```text
$ openclaw memory status --json        → stdout: []
$ openclaw memory search "query" --json → stdout: { "agentId": "main", "status": "disabled" }
```

The human-readable `openclaw memory status` prints the plain-text notice normally; under `--json` the notice line is rerouted to stderr by the runtime's json output mode, so stdout stays a parseable document — the missing disabled entries are the user-visible data gap.

## Expected

`memory status --json` includes disabled agents in the aggregate, e.g. `[{"agentId": "main", "status": "disabled"}]` — consistent with the search path's disabled shape and with the human output, so scripts can distinguish "no agents" from "all agents disabled".

## Version

Source checkout of `main` at `1c0ca31` (2026.11.3).

# Issue draft — HTML numeric entities 0x80–0x9F decode to raw C1 controls ## Summary `decodeHtmlEntities` (`src/shared/html-entities.ts`) decodes numeric character references in the 0x80–0x9F range with `String.fromCodePoint(codePoint)`, emitting raw Unicode C1 control characters (U+0080–U+009F) where the HTML5 numeric-character-reference end state maps this range through the windows-1252 table. Browsers and the vendored `entities` library apply that mapping, so OpenClaw text pipelines disagree with both. ## User-visible impact - `web_fetch` text extraction (`src/agents/tools/web-fetch-utils.ts` → `decodeEntities`) — a page containing `it’s a test — with “smart quotes” inside.` is delivered to the model as `it\x92s a test \x94 with \x93smart quotes\x9d inside.` — words fuse, quotes/dashes vanish into invisible controls. - Same decoder feeds Matrix mention parsing, MS Teams inbound text, DuckDuckGo result titles/snippets, and tool-call argument repair. ## Steps to reproduce 1. `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs -e "import {decodeHtmlEntities} from './src/shared/html-entities.ts'; console.log(JSON.stringify(decodeHtmlEntities('it’s a test — with “smart quotes” inside.')))"` on `main` → `"it\u0092s a test \u0094 with \u0093smart quotes\u009d inside."` 2. Same via the real extraction chain: `htmlToMarkdown('

it’s a test — with “smart quotes” inside.

', {extractMode:'text'})` → text with codepoints U+0092/U+0097/U+0093/U+0094. 3. HTML5/browsers/`entities` produce `it’s a test — with “smart quotes” inside.` (U+2019/U+2014/U+201C/U+201D). ## Expected Numeric references 0x80–0x9F decode through the windows-1252 end-state table (e.g. `’` → U+2019 `’`, `—` → U+2014 `—`, `“` → U+201C `“`, `€` → U+20AC `€`). Undefined cp1252 slots (0x81, 0x8D, 0x8F, 0x90, 0x9D) keep their C1 control, matching WHATWG. ## Version Source checkout of `main` at `1c0ca3120c5`.

## Problem

Managed local memory search still defaults to EmbeddingGemma 300M, and its pinned llama.cpp b10809 runtime predates EmbeddingGemma 2 support.

## Proposed scope

Upgrade the existing `llama-cpp` text embedding provider to the verified EmbeddingGemma 2 Q8_0 artifact and a compatible pinned runtime. Keep existing process ownership, transport, task prefixes, 768-dimensional vectors, and 2,048-token operating limits; do not add a provider, service, multimodal indexer, or configuration option.

The upgrade must migrate the shipped managed executable through Doctor, preserve explicit model choices/custom commands and preset tuning, and keep the old and new embedding spaces separate. Existing indexes using the previous default require a native rebuild. Direct-model services must explicitly identify the model they actually load.

Related: #186050 (broader Knowledge proposal; this request is limited to existing text-only memory search).

Public upstream references: [model card](https://huggingface.co/google/embeddinggemma-2), [GGUF artifact](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/embeddinggemma-2-GGUF), [llama.cpp v0.9.0](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/v0.9.0).

### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The Gateway intermittently becomes unresponsive on macOS and requires a restart. Two process samples taken during separate hangs show the main thread waiting for a write lock while closing a worker MessagePort.

### Steps to reproduce

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Expected behavior

The Gateway continues serving requests. Restarting the affected process restored service.

### Actual behavior

Three hangs were recorded on October 14–15. The process remained alive but the Gateway stopped responding. Samples from October 15 at 10:20 and 11:33 HKT show the same main-thread stack for every captured sample (1,808/1,808 and 1,360/1,360 respectively).

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.3, local source build `f6cf7bbb60c` (includes local carries, not an unmodified release).

### Operating system

macOS 26.6.1 (25G76), ARM64. Node 26; the captured library is `libnode.147.dylib`. The sample reports do not record the exact Node patch version.

### Install method

Git/source build, Gateway supervised by launchd.

### Model

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Provider / routing chain

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Logs

These excerpts come from `/usr/bin/sample` captures of two separate Gateway processes. Paths and addresses are omitted.

```text
2026-10-15 10:20:52 +0800, pid 22909
1808/1808 main-thread samples:
  node::HandleWrap::OnClose(uv_handle_s*)
  node::worker::MessagePort::OnClose()
  node::worker::SiblingGroup::Disentangle(node::worker::MessagePortData*)
  uv_rwlock_wrlock
  _pthread_rwlock_lock_slow
  _pthread_rwlock_lock_wait
  __psynch_rw_wrlock

2026-10-15 11:33:39 +0800, pid 22320
1360/1360 main-thread samples:
  node::HandleWrap::OnClose(uv_handle_s*)
  node::worker::MessagePort::OnClose()
  node::worker::SiblingGroup::Disentangle(node::worker::MessagePortData*)
  uv_rwlock_wrlock
  _pthread_rwlock_lock_slow
  _pthread_rwlock_lock_wait
  __psynch_rw_wrlock
```

### Impact and severity

One macOS Gateway installation; intermittent complete loss of service, requiring manual restart. Three incidents were recorded over two days. Frequency on other installations is unknown.

### Additional information

Related: #169535 (continuous V8 stall flight recorder).

Disabling only the flight recorder was deployed locally on October 15. No recurrence was recorded during the following 3.5-day observation period. This is an uncontrolled workaround observation, not proof of causation; there is no deterministic reproducer or re-enable/reproduce test.

Both hang samples contain a `v8:ProfEvntProc` thread, mostly in `SamplingEventsProcessor::Run` → `ConditionVariable::WaitFor`. Its presence does **not** establish that the profiler is deadlocked or owns the MessagePort lock. The samples establish the main-thread lock wait, not the lock owner or root cause.

Please investigate the MessagePort-close lock wait on macOS and whether continuous profiling contributes. This report does not propose merging the blanket recorder disable as a fix.

issues.body:
## Problem

A Talk agent consult started from the Gateway (the server realtime relay, run ids `talk-realtime-relay-consult-*`, and direct browser consults) does not run on the chat's configured runtime.

- If the chat's model runs on a CLI runtime (for example `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5` with `agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" }` and only a Claude CLI subscription login), typed messages in that chat work. A voice consult in the same chat fails with `No API key found for provider anthropic`, which surfaces as a "saved login looks expired" style message. The login is fine.
- If the chat's model selection is locked to a native harness (for example Codex), the voice consult is refused with `Model selection is locked for this session`.

The browser `talk.client.toolCall` path is not affected, because it already submits an internal `chat.send`.

## Cause

`src/gateway/talk/client-agent-runtime.ts` admits the consult and then calls the embedded runner (`runEmbeddedAgent`) directly. A typed turn goes through the agent command owner (`agentCommandFromGatewayIngress` → `runAgentAttempt`), which picks the Claude CLI backend, the native harness or the embedded runner for the session's model. Talk bypasses that selection, so it reaches the direct provider API. For locked sessions, `src/talk/agent-consult-runtime.ts` refuses up front because the embedded path cannot keep the native binding.

## Expected

A voice consult is a turn of the same chat: the same runtime, owner, sender and tool permissions as a typed message.

issues.body:
## Summary
Since the #83397 change, `sessions.list` with `configuredAgentsOnly: true` (the Control UI default) intentionally keeps ACP-keyed sessions (`agent:<acp-agent>:acp:<uuid>`) even when `<acp-agent>` is not in `agents.entries`. The sidebar shows them, but opening one or deleting it from the sidebar fails with `Unknown agent id "<acp-agent>"`. The row cannot be removed from the UI.

## Version
OpenClaw 2026.11.1 (4ffdd20), Linux, Gateway-hosted Control UI.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Config: `agents.entries` contains only ordinary agents (e.g. `main`); `acp.defaultAgent = "<acp-agent>"`, `acp.allowedAgents = ["<acp-agent>"]`; `<acp-agent>` is not an `agents.entries` key.
2. Spawn an ACP session from `main` (creates `agent:<acp-agent>:acp:<uuid>` in `agents/<acp-agent>/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite`).
3. Open the Control UI. The session appears in the sidebar (`/chat/<acp-agent>/<uuid-without-hyphens>`).
4. Click it, or delete it from the sidebar.

## Actual
- Open and sidebar delete both fail: `Unknown agent id "<acp-agent>"`.
- `openclaw sessions delete "agent:<acp-agent>:acp:<uuid>" --agent <acp-agent> --dry-run` fails the same way.
- `openclaw gateway call sessions.list --params '{"configuredAgentsOnly":true}'` still returns the row.

## Workaround
Delete by key without an explicit agent: `openclaw sessions delete "agent:<acp-agent>:acp:<uuid>" --yes` returns `deleted`. In `resolveRequestedSessionAgentId`, an agent-prefixed key without `agentId` only goes through database admission, but an explicit `agentId` must be in `listAgentIds(cfg)`. The Control UI always sends `agentId`, so it hits the second check.

## Expected
Sessions that `sessions.list` returns under `configuredAgentsOnly: true` can be opened, or at least deleted, from the Control UI.

## Suggested fixes (any one)
- Accept an explicit `agentId` that matches the key's agent when the store is a discovered ACP store (same admission as the key-only path), or have the UI omit `agentId` for agent-qualified keys.
- If such sessions are meant to be read-only, mark them in `sessions.list` so the UI shows them as such and still offers delete-by-key.
- `openclaw doctor`: report sessions/stores of agents that are neither in `agents.entries` nor ACP-allowed, and offer cleanup through the deletion journal.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On a personal install, `memory.search.rememberAcrossConversations` is effectively `true` (the docs say it "defaults on for personal installs"), but the bundled `active-memory` plugin that implements it is disabled by default (`openclaw plugins inspect active-memory` → `Reason: bundled (disabled by default)`). The docs for the setting say "Active Memory must remain enabled," yet nothing tells the user it isn't: setup, `openclaw doctor`, `openclaw doctor --lint` and the Control UI are all silent.

The result is that the agent looks configured to remember across conversations but never runs the recall pass. In our case this went unnoticed for about two months and showed up only as the agent seeming "forgetful" about things discussed in earlier conversations.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Personal install, `session.dmScope` unset, no `plugins.entries.active-memory` entry (the out-of-the-box state).
2. `memory.search.rememberAcrossConversations` is `true` (default, or set explicitly).
3. Run `openclaw plugins list`: Active Memory shows `disabled`.
4. Run `openclaw doctor` and `openclaw doctor --lint`: no finding about the mismatch.
5. Ask the agent about something from a previous conversation: no Active Memory recall runs (no `active-memory:` lines in the gateway log).

### Expected behavior

One of:
- Doctor (and ideally `openclaw memory status`) reports that `rememberAcrossConversations` is on but the `active-memory` plugin is disabled, and names the setting that fixes it. This would follow the pattern of #160320, which added a similar diagnostic for `memory.search.sources: ["sessions"]` being a silent no-op; or
- enabling `rememberAcrossConversations` (or having it default on) also enables the plugin, or setup offers to enable it.

### Actual behavior

The setting reads as enabled, the plugin stays disabled, and no surface reports the mismatch. After enabling the plugin (`plugins.entries.active-memory.enabled: true`, hot-applied, no restart), recall started working immediately: the gateway log shows `active-memory: … start timeoutMs=15000` followed by `done status=ok elapsedMs≈5400 summaryChars≈200`, and the agent answered questions about earlier conversations correctly, citing the right memory note.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.7 (157d8c2). The setting has been present in our config since early October (2026.9.x); the plugin was never enabled in any config version since then.

### Operating system

Windows 11 + WSL2 (Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS), Node 26.12.1, gateway as a systemd user service

### Install method

npm (global), updated via the managed updater

### Model

openai/gpt-5.6-terra (main and Active Memory recall)

### Provider / routing chain

OpenAI primary, Anthropic fallback. Memory search: `provider: "local"` (managed llama.cpp provider, EmbeddingGemma-300M QAT Q8_0), sources memory + sessions.

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell
[reload] config hot reload applied (plugins.entries.active-memory)
[plugins] active-memory: agent=main session=agent:main:dashboard:<id> ... start timeoutMs=15000 queryChars=440 searchQueryChars=63
[plugins] active-memory: recall skipped reason=session-ineligible
[plugins] active-memory: agent=main session=agent:main:dashboard:<id> ... done status=ok elapsedMs=5412 summaryChars=175
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Medium. Likely affects most personal installs that never enabled the plugin by hand. Nothing breaks, but cross-conversation recall (the main benefit of the setting) silently never runs, so users experience an agent that forgets earlier conversations and have no diagnostic pointing to the cause.

### Additional information

Related question (Control UI chats):

With the plugin enabled, every Control UI dashboard chat we tested (`agent:main:dashboard:<id>`, an existing one and a fresh one from `/new`) logs `active-memory: recall skipped reason=session-ineligible` for the cross-conversation transcript lane, while the memory lookup itself runs. The docs limit that lane to "private direct or persistent explicit UI conversations," but don't say how dashboard chats are classified. For a single-operator personal install, the Control UI is the main place people talk to their agent. Is excluding dashboard chats intended? If so, could the docs say so, and could `/active-memory status` show the reason?

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On a git-checkout install with an explicit updater temporary directory, `updater-runtime-retention` hard-linked 0 files and byte-copied all 162,786, taking 222 s before the update reached preflight.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Linux host, git-checkout install, with the install and the configured updater temporary directory on different mounts of a Btrfs data volume (the snapshot-space preflight reports the temporary directory as `explicit-tmpdir`).
2. Stop the Gateway service.
3. Run `openclaw update --channel dev --yes --json`.
4. Read the `updater-runtime-retention` step diagnostics in the JSON result.

Observed once on this host. The mount layout of the two paths was not captured with `findmnt`, so the cross-device cause below is not confirmed.

### Expected behavior

`src/infra/update-retained-runtime-tree.ts` documents retention as hard-linking the admitted tree, copying bytes only when the filesystem refuses the link or the member is rewritten for relocation. PR #155977 (`fix(update): retain the running updater by hard link instead of copying the package`) set that as the intended behavior. A retention that falls back to copying the whole package should either avoid the fallback or report why it happened.

### Actual behavior

Every file was copied and nothing in the output says why:

```
[update/retained-runtime] Runtime retention attempt 1/1: preparing the running updater
[update/retained-runtime] runtime retention attempt 1/1: dependency inventory
[update/retained-runtime] runtime retention attempt 1/1: materializing 184723 entries (4299464704 estimated bytes) after 82674ms inventory
```

Step diagnostics:

```json
{"entries":184723,"estimatedBytes":4299464704,"inventoryMs":82674,"materializationMs":134202,"linked":0,"copied":162786}
```

`updater-runtime-retention` `durationMs` was 222474 of a 961527 ms run.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.10 (git checkout; upstream base `aedae9dc` plus 3 local commits in gateway/state identity code; no updater file is known to differ, not exhaustively checked)

### Operating system

Linux (distribution not recorded), Btrfs data volume

### Install method

git checkout, dev channel, systemd-managed Gateway

### Model

N/A (updater path)

### Provider / routing chain

N/A (updater path)

### Logs

```shell
# snapshot-space-preflight, same run
explicit-tmpdir <updater-tmp>: 18 GiB needed; 997 GiB free.
system-tmpdir /tmp: 18 GiB needed; 8.7 GiB free.
```

### Impact and severity

- Affected: git-checkout installs whose explicit updater temporary directory is not hard-linkable from the install.
- Severity: annoying to blocking. 222 s and about 4.3 GB of writes per update attempt, before any check that can reject the update.
- Frequency: 1/1 observed attempts with this configuration.
- Consequence: each failed attempt pays the full copy again. Earlier attempts on this host left `openclaw-update-runtime-*` directories next to the install, and this attempt's log listed about 39 retained directories that cleanup skipped because another OpenClaw process was still running.

### Additional information

Reading of current `main` (`89c5b179`), not confirmed on the host:

- `src/infra/update-retained-runtime.ts` only places the retained directory beside the install when no temporary root is configured (`!temporaryRoot && ... sourceStat.dev === parentStat.dev`). With an explicit temporary root it always uses that root, with no device check.
- `src/infra/update-retained-runtime-tree.ts` treats `EXDEV` as link-unsupported and falls back to `copyEntry` per file.
- On Btrfs, separate subvolumes report different `st_dev`, so the same-device test and `link(2)` both fail across subvolumes of one filesystem even though a reflink clone would succeed there.

Possible directions: prefer a same-device directory beside the install even when a temporary root is configured, attempt a reflink clone before a byte copy, and log one line when retention degrades to copying (count and first errno).

Related but different: #171446 (closed, retention loop on a package install), #182616 (SQLite copy cost).

issues.body:
### Summary

Reduce the wall time of `openclaw backup create --verify` on large installs. Today it takes 23 to 25 minutes for a 16 GB archive on an Apple-silicon Mac mini with internal NVMe, and on an install with PostgreSQL stores the Gateway is down for all of it.

### Problem to solve

Whole-installation backups that include any PostgreSQL store need offline custody (`docs/gateway/postgresql.md:433-435`). Our install has the workboard store on PostgreSQL, so before every update and every `database port` we stop the Gateway and take a matched archive with `openclaw backup create --verify`. That step is our own runbook, but it follows from the offline-custody rule, and it is now the largest part of our planned downtime. It is longer than the update itself: `openclaw update` validation took 835 to 910 s in the same runs.

Four runs on the same machine, from our maintenance logs:

| date | start → end | elapsed | archive |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 2026-10-23 | 18:56 → 19:19 | ~23 min | 15.9 GB |
| 2026-10-24 | 05:00:05 → 05:24:54 | 24 min 49 s | 15.9 GB |
| 2026-10-24 | 14:09:37 → 14:34:12 | 24 min 35 s | 16.1 GB |
| 2026-10-24 | 15:09:18 → 15:34:34 | 25 min 16 s | 16.1 GB |

The archive covers the state directory, including the agent and shared SQLite stores (about 5.3 GB of SQLite, the largest file 4.1 GB), the workspace, the PostgreSQL capsule for the workboard store, and other files under the state directory. We have not timed the create and verify phases separately.

What the current code does for one run, as we read it on main (dcb918e167a; only a trivial timer cleanup in `backup-create-stream.ts` changed since our build 98f1a668):

1. **Create, SQLite snapshots:** each SQLite store is first copied to a private temp directory (`src/infra/backup-create.ts:336-365`).
2. **Create, compression:** one tar traversal goes into one `createGzip()` stream at default options (`src/infra/backup-create-stream.ts:14-34`, `appendBackupManifest`; called from `backup-create.ts:578-600`). A single zlib stream compresses one chunk at a time, so compression uses one thread.
3. **Verify** (`src/commands/backup.ts:56-58` → `verifyBackupArchive`):
   - `listBackupArchiveEntries` runs `tar.t` with `gzip: true` over the whole archive (`src/commands/backup-verify-manifest.ts:599-640`, called at `src/commands/backup-verify.ts:509`). #175518 already folded the manifest read into this pass.
   - When PostgreSQL captures exist, `verifyPostgresSnapshots` (called at `backup-verify.ts:638`) extracts its artifacts with `extractDatabaseArtifacts`, which is `tar.x` with `gzip: true` and a filter (`backup-verify.ts:267-299`, called at line 320). The filter selects entries, but the whole archive is still decompressed to reach them.
   - `verifySqliteSnapshots` (line 639) calls `extractDatabaseArtifacts` again for each batch of SQLite snapshots (lines 391-397). That is another full decompression pass, and more if the global database registers agent stores the manifest did not declare.
   - Each extracted SQLite snapshot gets a full `PRAGMA integrity_check` (`assertSqliteIntegrity`, `backup-verify.ts:418`; default check in `src/infra/sqlite-integrity.ts:216`). The `main` agent snapshot alone is 4.1 GB.

So a verified backup on an install with PostgreSQL stores decompresses the full 16 GB archive at least three times, after compressing it once on one thread. It also re-reads and integrity-checks SQLite images that the same command had just made with SQLite's own snapshot API.

### Proposed solution

These are ideas only. We have not measured any of them, and we don't know how the 25 minutes split between the steps above.

1. **One extraction pass in verify:** collect the PostgreSQL capsule artifacts and the declared SQLite snapshots during the listing pass, then extract them in a single `tar.x` (or stream them out during `tar.t`). This removes at least one full decompression pass. A second batch would only be needed for agent stores that the manifest did not declare.
2. **Verify while creating:** for `create --verify`, check the staged SQLite and PostgreSQL images in the temp directory before or while they stream into the archive. Verification then only has to confirm that the archive holds the same bytes, for example with a hash computed while writing and checked during the listing pass. This removes the extract-and-recheck round trip. Standalone `backup verify` would keep today's full path.
3. **Compression:** a faster codec or parallel compression would cut both the create pass and each verify pass. #182699 already proposes opt-in zstd, with measurements, so we do not repeat that here. With three decompression passes in verify, a faster decoder counts several times over on this path.
4. **Unchanged store snapshots:** most of the 5.3 GB of SQLite does not change between two backups taken an hour apart. Skipping re-compression of unchanged snapshots is the deduplication idea in #155599, and is probably a larger change than 1 and 2.

### Alternatives considered

- Taking the archive with the Gateway running is not available while any store is on PostgreSQL (offline custody).
- `backup create` without `--verify` saves the verify passes, but we then hand an unverified archive to the update or port as its rollback point. We prefer not to.
- Excluding large directories from the archive would cut size, but the matched archive is meant to be the whole installation.

### Impact

- Affected: installs with PostgreSQL stores that take matched offline archives before maintenance. The same verify cost applies to any large `backup create --verify`.
- Severity: planned downtime. On our install, each update costs about 25 minutes of archive time on top of about 15 to 20 minutes of `openclaw update` itself.
- Frequency: every update and every `database port`. That was 4 times in 2 days for us.
- Consequence: the Gateway, and every channel on it, is offline for the whole archive step.

### Evidence/examples

The timings in the table above come from our maintenance wrapper. It logs a timestamp before `openclaw backup create --output <dir> --verify` and another when the command returns. For example, from the 2026-10-24 05:00 run (paths shortened):

```
05:00:05 running: openclaw backup create --output ~/Library/Backups/openclaw-archive --verify
05:24:54 archive: ~/Library/Backups/openclaw-archive/2026-10-24T05-00-06.463-07-00-openclaw-backup.tar.gz ( 15G, verified)
```

Code references are listed under "Problem to solve". Host: Apple-silicon Mac mini, 16 GB RAM, internal NVMe, macOS (Darwin 27). OpenClaw 2026.10.6 (main 98f1a668); source checked against main dcb918e167a.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

Duplicate search (`gh search issues --repo openclaw/openclaw --include-prs`): "backup create slow", "backup verify slow", "backup zstd", "backup gzip", "backup compression", "backup create --verify", "offline backup downtime postgres", "backup parallel compression", "backup verify decompress". Related:

- #182699: opt-in zstd for backup archives. This covers our compression idea; the request here is about the repeated verify passes and the downtime framing.
- #175518: removed the separate manifest re-read in verify.
- #155599: backup deduplication.

None of the existing issues covers the repeated full-archive decompression in `create --verify`.

If it helps, we can time the create and verify phases separately on this install, and the listing and extraction passes inside verify.

issues.body:
## Summary

`video_generate` with `openrouter/google/veo-3.1-fast` fails with
`HTTP 401: User not found` on **every** attempt, while the same API key
succeeds against the same endpoint via direct `curl` (`202 Accepted`).

The failure is invariant across every user-side variable: inline key, SecretRef,
OAuth-style auth profile, `env`-kind secret, `secret`-kind host-bound secret,
clean process environment, and gateway restarts. This appears to be the media-generation
variant of #166137 (unsubstituted/stale credentials reaching upstream), which I hit
directly in a related form (see "Reproduced the same class of failure" below).

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.11.3 (847611d)`
- Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, kernel `7.0.0-43-generic`, Node `v26.13.1`
- Gateway: mode `local`, bind `lan`, port `18789`
- Provider: `models.providers.openrouter`, `baseUrl: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`
- Model: `openrouter/google/veo-3.1-fast`
- `secrets.egressProxy.enabled: true`, `secrets.providers: {}`

## Reproduction

1. Configure OpenRouter with a valid API key.
2. Call `video_generate` with `model: openrouter/google/veo-3.1-fast`, a prompt, and an input image.
3. Result: `OpenRouter video generation failed (HTTP 401): User not found.`

## Evidence

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `POST /api/v1/videos` via curl, key from config | **202 Accepted** |
| `POST /api/v1/videos` via curl, key read from gateway `/proc/PID/environ` | **202 Accepted** |
| `GET /api/v1/key` with same key | **200** |
| `video_generate` tool, same config and key | **401 User not found** |

Credential configurations attempted, all failing identically:

1. **Inline literal** — `models.providers.openrouter.apiKey: "sk-or-v1-..."`. Confirmed on disk before and after restart.
2. **SecretRef** — `{"source":"store","provider":"default","id":"OPENROUTER_API_KEY"}`.
3. **Auth profile** — `openclaw models auth login --provider openrouter --method api-key`, creating `openrouter:default [openrouter/api_key]`. `openclaw models auth list` reports the profile exists, but `auth_profile_store` in the agent DB contains **0 rows**.
4. **`env`-kind store entry**, then **`secret`-kind host-bound entry** (`--kind secret --allow-host openrouter.ai`), matching the shape of every other working provider key in the same store (`DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `PGS_GROVE_API_KEY`, `TAVILY_API_KEY` — all `secret`, write-only, host-bound). OpenRouter was the sole outlier and still failed after being normalized.

## Eliminated

- **Endpoint** — `dist/video-generation-provider-DwNE9Ftu.mjs` posts to `${baseUrl}/videos`, identical to the working curl.
- **Request body** — `buildRequestBody()` emits `model`, `prompt`, `duration`, `aspect_ratio`, `frame_images`; equivalent curl body succeeded.
- **Process environment** — a systemd drop-in supplying `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` was removed; `/proc/PID/environ` has **zero** `OPENROUTER` entries and the failure is unchanged, ruling out env-precedence issues.
- **Network** — `GET https://api.github.com/rate_limit` → 200; `POST /api/v1/videos` unauth → proper 401 from OpenRouter. Outbound connectivity is healthy.
- **Egress proxy allowlist** — `secrets.providers` empty, `proxy.worker.js` running, host-bound secret registered for `openrouter.ai`.

## Reproduced the same class of failure via `gh`

Attempting `gh issue create --repo openclaw/openclaw` from exec, and via raw
`curl` using the token from `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`, both returned:

```
HTTP 502  Secret egress proxy refused an unresolved secret sentinel
```

Meanwhile `curl` without auth returned a normal `401 Requires authentication`
from GitHub. So the network and request path are fine; **only requests carrying a
stored credential are refused/fail**. This strongly suggests the video 401 is the
same substitution failure, failing silently (upstream sees an unresolved sentinel
and reports "User not found") rather than loudly.

## Suspected area

`generateVideo()` → `resolveOpenRouterGenerationRequestContext()`
(`dist/generation-request-context-fXMPfOdS.mjs`) → `resolveApiKeyForProvider()`
→ `resolveProviderRuntimeApiKey()` → `resolveApiKeyForProviderCore()`
(`dist/model-auth-provider-CQhmXGGd.mjs`).

Header construction:

```js
Authorization: `Bearer ${auth.apiKey}`
```

Given the configured key is independently proven valid, the value returned for
`capability: "video"` either differs from the configured credential or is a
sentinel the egress proxy fails to substitute on this path.

## Related issues

- #166137 — egress proxy sentinel substitution intermittently ineffective; calls reach upstream APIs with unsubstituted credentials (401)
- #147620 — egress proxy cannot substitute sentinels inside HTTP Basic credentials
- #194306 — Basic auth rejects protected sentinel for pre-encoded payload (502 unresolved secret)
- #136734 — egress proxy does not substitute store-secret sentinels in HTTPS request headers from exec (closed; independently re-reproduced in comments)
- #79535 — OpenRouter video generation silently fails (older, different symptom: no error at all)

## Ask

1. Is there a supported way to log the resolved `auth.apiKey` for the media-generation capability path?
2. Does `secrets` sentinelization apply to media-generation requests, and can an unresolved sentinel reach an `Authorization` header there (yielding upstream 401 rather than a loud proxy refusal)?
3. Is `credentialPrecedence` honoured for media generation, or does it use a separate resolution chain?

issues.body:
**Version:** OpenClaw 2026.9.8 (fc23bc8), Claude Code 2.1.322, macOS.

**What happens:** a `chat.send` with `queueMode: "steer"` during a running claude-cli turn is acked, then admitted as a separate turn after the current run ends. The running reply never sees it. On the embedded runtime (for example xai models) the same steer joins the reply at the next tool or model boundary.

**Why it looks fixable:** the live session already starts Claude Code with `--print --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --replay-user-messages` and keeps stdin open (cli-runtime-args, cli-live-session-registry). Verified 2026-11-14 with Claude Code 2.1.322 alone (no OpenClaw): a turn running a foreground `sleep 25` received a second stream-json user message at 9.1 s and ended as ONE turn answering the steered instruction (`STEERED`, single result event, the original `FIRST` never sent). So the live process already supports steering; only the gateway's routing is missing.

**Ask:** route `steer` on a live claude-cli session to a stream-json user message written to that process's stdin, and report it through the same pending-input row lifecycle the embedded runtime uses. Fall back to the current followup behaviour when no live process is attached.

**Repro:** start a claude-cli turn that runs `sleep 90` before writing text, send a steer "reply only with STEERED" 10 s in. Expected: the reply after the sleep reflects the steer. Actual: the original reply finishes, then a second turn answers STEERED.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

When a tool call fails and its output contains a token or API key, safeguard compaction stores that text unredacted in the summary's `## Tool Failures` section, while the excerpt of the same tool result in the summary is redacted.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start an isolated Gateway (`pnpm openclaw gateway run --bind loopback`) on `main` with `agents.defaults.compaction.mode: "safeguard"` and a scripted OpenAI-compatible model.
2. In one session, run a turn where the agent calls `exec` with an `echo` of a synthetic `token` assignment and a synthetic `sk-` key (both carry the marker `FAKEE2E`) followed by `sleep 30`, and `timeoutSeconds: 2`, so the call fails with a timeout after printing those synthetic values.
3. Run `openclaw sessions compact <session-key> --json`.
4. Look at the summary in the compact reply (the stored compaction entry in the agent database holds the same text), and send one more turn.

### Expected behavior

The `## Tool Failures` line redacts the values, as the excerpt of the same tool result already does: `- exec (status=failed): connecting with [redacted] [redacted] Command timed out after 2 seconds. ...`. The compaction docs (`docs/concepts/compaction.md`) say the same credential redaction applies to every text the summary quotes from the conversation.

### Actual behavior

(The synthetic `token` assignment and `sk-` key are shown as `<synthetic token assignment>` and `<synthetic sk- key>`, and the summary heading line as `Tool Failures section:`; the marker counts are read from the unedited run.)

The summary in the `sessions compact --json` reply quotes both values raw in the failure line, and the next model request carries them. Below: the `## Tool Failures` heading and its one entry, the preserved tool-result line of the same call, the marker count over the whole summary, and the marker count in the first model request after compaction. Left out: the turn and compact exit lines (all 0), the rest of the summary, and the same lines read from the stored compaction entry in a copy of the agent database, which match the reply (2 markers).

```text
[... turn and compact exit lines left out ...]
Tool Failures section:
- exec (status=failed): connecting with <synthetic token assignment> <synthetic sk- key> Command timed out after 2 seconds. The command was terminated, but external side effects may already have completed. Verify the resulting state before retryi...
- Tool result (exec): connecting with [redacted] [redacted]
FAKEE2E markers in stored summary: 2
request after compaction: roles=system,user,assistant,user,user; FAKEE2E markers sent to the model: 2; tool messages: 0
[... database read of the same entry left out; same lines, 2 markers ...]
```

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.3 (`main` at 8aa2434748a)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS

### Install method

pnpm dev (source checkout)

### Model

mock/mock-model (a scripted OpenAI-compatible endpoint on loopback)

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> local scripted OpenAI-compatible endpoint (openai-completions)

### Additional provider/model setup details

The model was scripted so that the failing tool call happens on demand. The `## Tool Failures` section is built from the transcript before the summary model is called, so the provider does not affect it.

### Logs

```shell
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The output above was read from the summary in the compact reply, from a copy of the agent database in the isolated state directory (same lines), and from the next request the Gateway sent to the model endpoint.

### Impact and severity

Affected: sessions using safeguard compaction (the default for new configs) where a failed tool call printed a credential.
Severity: the compaction summary keeps the credential-shaped value and replays it to the model after compaction, while the same tool result's excerpt elsewhere in the summary is redacted.
Frequency: 1/1 observed run on `main` `8aa2434748a`.
Consequence: in that run, the value was stored in the summary and sent in the first model request after compaction.

### Additional information

Credential redaction for compaction summary text was added in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/197349. The Tool Failures line is a quoted text it does not reach.

issues.body:
After `COPY . .`, the `build` stage of `Dockerfile` runs two chmod steps:

```dockerfile
RUN find /app -path /app/node_modules -prune -o -exec chmod a+rX {} +
RUN for dir in /app/${OPENCLAW_BUNDLED_PLUGIN_DIR} /app/.agent /app/.agents; do \
      if [ -d "$dir" ]; then \
        find "$dir" -type d -exec chmod 755 {} +; \
        find "$dir" -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +; \
      fi; \
    done
```

On overlayfs-backed BuildKit, `chmod` copies each file it touches up into the new layer, even when the mode is already correct. These steps touch about 62k entries and cost about 800 MB of I/O each time `COPY . .` misses the cache, and the resulting layer is the same either way (0 B for the first step). On our remote builder they take 278 s and 47 s; on an 8-core local Docker they take 63 s and 16 s.

**Suggested fix:** chmod only the entries whose mode would change.

```dockerfile
RUN find /app -path /app/node_modules -prune -o \( -type d ! -perm -0555 -o -type f \( ! -perm -0444 -o -perm /0111 ! -perm -0111 \) \) -exec chmod a+rX {} +
```

and in the extensions loop, `-type d ! -perm 0755 -exec chmod 755 {} +` and `-type f ! -perm 0644 -exec chmod 644 {} +`.

**Verification** at 1f5b1d10c403bb5c5e0a3ead9b342be3a4444180:
- A dump of `find /app -printf '%m %u:%g %y %p\n'` is identical before and after the change across all 62,409 entries. A synthetic tree with 000, 100, 600, 744, 4755, 2750 and 1777 files and 0500/0700 directories also gives identical modes.
- The two steps drop from 62.7 s and 16.3 s to 1.3 s and 0.5 s locally. On our CI builder the full base build is about 5.4 minutes faster on a cache miss.
- One behavior difference: a dangling symlink makes the current step fail with "cannot operate on dangling symlink", while the narrowed `find` skips it. The tree has no dangling links today.

We carry this as a Dockerfile patch in our build until upstream has it.

issues.body:
## Bug

In `apps/android/app/src/main/java/ai/openclaw/app/node/CameraCaptureManager.kt`, `attachActivity(activity: ComponentActivity)` stores a strong reference to `contextActivity` without observing the activity's `ON_DESTROY` lifecycle event to clear it.

## Impact

Across configuration changes or activity destruction, `CameraCaptureManager` retains the destroyed `ComponentActivity` instance and can bind `ProcessCameraProvider` against a destroyed lifecycle owner if a new activity has not yet re-attached.

## Fix

Track a `DefaultLifecycleObserver` on the attached `ComponentActivity` in `CameraCaptureManager.attachActivity` that clears `contextActivity` when that exact activity reaches `onDestroy`.

The fix is ready on `saariuslystoned/openclaw:fix/android-camera-retire-destroyed-activity-20261108` at `d38c7c12db5e61c273486053908709dcfe691b4c` ☁️

issues.body:
### Summary

A stable, incremental Gateway export of per-call usage records (with archived and deleted sessions), so external dashboards can stop reading OpenClaw's internal SQLite tables.

### Problem to solve

`usage.cost` gives daily totals and `sessions.usage` gives per-session usage, which covers the built-in Usage view. A self-hosted dashboard that keeps its own long-term history needs more than that: per-call records it can fold by hour, model, agent and reasoning or harness settings, tool call counts, and usage from sessions that were later archived or deleted. Today the only way to get those is to read `openclaw-agent.sqlite` tables (`session_windows`, `trajectory_runtime_events`, `session_transcript_archives` with zstd frames) directly.

Those tables are internal and can change in any release; a one-way database migration can silently break such readers, so every upgrade has to be preceded by testing them against a migrated copy.

### Proposed solution

A read-only Gateway method (and matching CLI) that streams usage records after a cursor, for example `usage.records` with `{ "after": "<cursor>", "limit": 1000 }` returning `{ "records": [...], "next": "<cursor>" }`:

- one record per model call: timestamp, agent id, session kind (direct, cron, sub-agent), provider, model, input, output, cache read and cache write tokens, reasoning level and harness or fast mode when known, and the tool calls it made (names and counts only, never arguments or content);
- archived and deleted sessions included, with a stable record id so consumers can deduplicate;
- a schema version, and a documented guarantee that a migration keeps the cursor and record ids valid.

### Alternatives considered

- Parsing `sessions.usage` per session: no per-call grain, no tool counts, and deleted sessions disappear.
- Reading the SQLite stores: works, but depends on internal schemas that migrations may change.
- OpenTelemetry export: needs an extra collector and still does not cover history written before it was enabled.

### Impact

Anyone running an external usage or cost dashboard over OpenClaw. With a stable export, upgrades stop needing a reader requalification step, and the dashboard cannot undercount silently after a migration.

### Evidence/examples

Our dashboard reads the three tables above every minute. A pre-upgrade check now has to run that reader against a copy of the home migrated by the candidate version before each OpenClaw update.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No.

issues.body:
## Summary

A `sessions_send` message to a session whose turn is currently running is accepted, then rejected 4 ms later with `ActiveTurnClaimError`, and ends up in `session_pending_inputs` as `state='interrupted'`. It is never replayed, not even after the running turn ends, and the sender only ever sees the accepted/queued result.

## Version

- Observed on OpenClaw **2026.11.3** (`847611d`), macOS arm64, single gateway, embedded runtime.
- `main` checked at `92016ce978f0f638369ecd0d10fcaa9212e591ce`: the local-placement admission path still rejects immediately (see Root cause). I have not run a live repro on `main` yet.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start a session with a long turn, e.g. an isolated cron job (`agentTurn`) that runs for a few minutes.
2. While that turn is running, call `sessions_send` from another session targeting the cron session key.
3. Let the cron turn finish.
4. Inspect the target agent DB:
   ```sql
   SELECT input_id, state, consumed_event_id, accepted_at
   FROM session_pending_inputs
   WHERE session_key = '<target-session-key>'
   ORDER BY seq DESC LIMIT 5;
   ```

## Expected

Either the message is queued and delivered as the next turn once the claim is released (as `messages.queue` does for channel ingress), or `sessions_send` returns a clear failure so the sender can retry.

## Actual

Gateway log at the moment of the send (ids anonymised):

```
2026-11-15T01:34:48.552+02:00 [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=session:agent:main:cron:<job-id> durationMs=4 error="Session <session-id> already has an active turn claim" errorName=ActiveTurnClaimError
```

The pending-input row:

```
accepted_at          session_key                 state        consumed_event_id  provenance
2026-11-15 01:34:48  agent:main:cron:<job-id>    interrupted  NULL               inter_session (sessions_send)
```

It is still `interrupted` long after the cron turn ended; nothing replays it. The sender got an accepted result and no later failure.

State totals in one agent DB over a few weeks: `interrupted: 79`, `cancelled: 179`, `queued: 1`, all with `consumed_event_id IS NULL`. Several of the `interrupted` rows are `inter_session` messages from `sessions_send` (to dashboard and cron sessions).

`sessions_history` documents the current behaviour ("Cancelled inputs never replay; interrupted means saved without an active retry."), so the input is kept, but no path ever retries it and nobody is told.

## Root cause (as far as I can trace it)

- For local placements, a second turn that hits an existing claim is rejected right away. It only waits for release if the holder is already being cancelled or a worker result is reconciling:
  https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/92016ce978f0f638369ecd0d10fcaa9212e591ce/src/gateway/worker-environments/worker-turn-admission.ts#L589-L638
  https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/92016ce978f0f638369ecd0d10fcaa9212e591ce/src/gateway/worker-environments/placement-local-turns.ts#L75-L85
- The accepted input is then settled through the pending-input owner's `finish(disposition)`, which persists `interrupted` / `cancelled` and releases the owner. Nothing schedules a replay for `interrupted` afterwards:
  https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/92016ce978f0f638369ecd0d10fcaa9212e591ce/src/config/sessions/session-accessor.pending-inputs.ts#L470-L520

I could not pin the exact caller that picks `interrupted` (rather than `cancelled`) for this lane-error path, so please correct me if the settlement happens somewhere else.

## Related

- #168404: same symptom on the `agent` RPC path (closed 2026-10-10). On 2026.11.3 the input is now retained, but it still is never delivered.
- #176330: `ActiveTurnClaimError` instead of followup queueing for cron wakes / second surfaces on DM sessions (closed).
- #196656: lost subagent completion announces.

## Possible fix shapes (smallest first)

1. When admission fails with `ActiveTurnClaimError` for an inter-session / programmatic send, keep the input `queued` and wait for `waitForTurnClaimRelease` (as is already done for the cancellation case), then run it.
2. Leave admission as is, but have turn-claim release drain `queued`/`interrupted` inputs of that session that have no `consumed_event_id`.
3. At minimum, report the rejection back to the `sessions_send` caller (status `error` with the claim reason) instead of accepted, so the sender can retry.

Happy to test a fix against this setup.
