prs.title: feat(infra): LiteLLM provider gateway as OpenClaw fallback
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw had no provider fallback path: every request went to a single provider, so an outage or a quota error on that provider surfaced directly to the user with no second attempt. There was also no supervision for such a gateway — a silently dead gateway looks exactly like a healthy one until a user hits it. On top of that, gateway traffic carried no session-level attribution: token usage and cost could not be tied back to the agent session that produced them.

This PR adds the fallback gateway with the supervision that keeps it honest, and the tracing that ties gateway traffic back to sessions, routes and cost.

## Solution

Adds LiteLLM as an OpenClaw fallback provider gateway, with the pieces required to actually run it:

- `litellm.config.yaml` — 35 model aliases over NVIDIA NIM (MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Nemotron fast/lightning/vl), OpenRouter (MiniMax, GLM), DeepInfra and the rest, so providers can be swapped without touching OpenClaw.
- `docker-compose.litellm.yml` — the gateway service on port 4000, config mounted read-only.
- `litellm-health-monitor.sh` plus `deploy/systemd/litellm-health-monitor.{service,timer}` — health probe that alerts and restarts a dead gateway (3-minute timer).
- `litellm_callbacks/langfuse_trace_context.py` — LiteLLM callback that re-attaches the agent session id and agent name to the Langfuse trace, so tokens and cost land on the right session instead of an anonymous trace.
- `litellm-test.sh` — smoke test for the alias set.
- `scripts/add-nvidia-key-interactive.sh`, `scripts/add-mplan-key-interactive.sh` — interactive wallet-backed key installation for the two providers that need it.
- `LITELLM_GATEWAY.md`, `.env.example` — operator docs and the environment contract.

`litellm_settings.callbacks` is wired to `["langfuse_trace_context", "langfuse_otel"]`, in the order the callback module itself prescribes. Fallback chains cover `claude-opus-4-5`, `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` and `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` alongside the existing routes.

### Langfuse tracing and gateway attribution

- `diagnostics.langfuse` is a new config section: enabling it points the existing OTEL exporter at the Langfuse OTLP ingress (traces only, metrics and logs stay off) with Basic auth, the ingestion-version header and the environment label on the resource. `capturePrompts` stays off unless explicitly enabled.
- An unreachable Langfuse collector degrades to "no export" instead of failing the plugin service; an incomplete Langfuse configuration reports `langfuse_config_incomplete` through the exporter-health event instead of exporting to a broken endpoint.
- Harness runs now report the route that served them (`provider/model`), whether the gateway fell back, the runner type, the gateway request id, the token usage and the cost, on both the diagnostic event and the exported span.

## Impact

- New files plus focused additions; no existing runtime path is replaced.
- The gateway runs as a separate container; OpenClaw reaches it over `http://localhost:4000` and its master key comes from the environment.
- Keys are installed through the secret wallet; the interactive scripts read the token from a prompt and never echo it.
- The new `diagnostics.langfuse` section is optional and inert unless enabled; `capturePrompts` defaults to off.

## Evidence

- `litellm.config.yaml` parses cleanly (35 models, callbacks registered).
- `bash -n` passes for `litellm-test.sh`, `litellm-health-monitor.sh`, `scripts/add-nvidia-key-interactive.sh`, `scripts/add-mplan-key-interactive.sh`; `py_compile` passes for the Langfuse callback.
- Gateway health-check reports `secret-wallet-ok`; live requests through the `nvidia-minimax` and `nvidia-nemotron-fast` aliases return HTTP 200.
- Key placement reconciled against the wallet: `wallet.py reconcile --project openclaw-litellm` → 7/7 MATCH, `Overall: PASS`.
- The interactive wallet scripts were exercised end to end: the token is read from the prompt, written to the wallet, and the old value is backed up before replacement.
- Typecheck on the touched packages is green (`tsgo:core`, `tsgo:extensions`, and the `test-root` shards); the affected test files pass — `extensions/diagnostics-otel/src/service.test.ts` 74 passed / 1 failed, where the single failure (`records message-flow metrics and spans`) reproduces unchanged on a clean checkout of this branch's base. `src/config/config.diagnostics.test.ts` and `src/agents/harness/lifecycle.test.ts` pass.

## Notes for reviewers

- The branch was rebased onto `origin/main` and narrowed to the commits that transplant cleanly. Two earlier commits that touched the Telegram native-command layer and the image-generation provider registry were deliberately left out: upstream restructured both subsystems since these were written, so they need a deliberate port rather than a patch transplant. They are not lost — they remain available as a follow-up branch.
- The `AGENTS.md` conflict was resolved following this repository's own convention ("put long rules in the owning guide and leave a one-line pointer here"): the evidence-only reporting rules now live in `.agents/skills/openclaw-testing/SKILL.md` under `#report-only-evidenced-results`, and `AGENTS.md` carries a single pointer to them.
- The Langfuse tracing and gateway-attribution work was re-based onto the current upstream layout by hand: the diagnostics extension is now split into `service.ts` / `service-traces.ts` / `service-recorders-*.ts`, the config schema lives in `zod-schema.logging.ts`, and the harness lifecycle lives in `src/agents/harness/lifecycle.ts`. Identity fields (`run_id`, `session_id`) stay off exported spans, as this repository's attribute-redaction policy requires.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The composer **Waiting on `<command>`** card added in #198891 shows the same running commands that the session **Details** panel already lists under **Processes**, next to **View all processes** and **Subagents**. Two places now report the same background work.

## User Impact

The card above the composer is gone. The running background command still appears in **Details → Processes**, where it opens its output and **Stop** is available. Exec completion wakes are unchanged: the agent still continues the chat when the command exits.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Removes the card component, its test, its lazy mount in the composer, its selectors in `composer-progress.css`, its three English strings and its docs sentences (`docs/web/control-ui/chat.md`, `docs/gateway/background-process.md`, including the adopted-process mention added later in #199222).
- Removes the optional `wakesSession` field from `sessions.processes.list` rows. Only the card read it: no other reference exists in `ui`, `apps/macos`, `apps/ios`, `apps/android`, `extensions` or `src`, and the Swift and Kotlin protocol models never included it. It is not in any release: `git tag --contains a519dcf` lists no `v*` tag (`v2026.11.5-beta.3` does not contain it). Main and beta are not shipped contracts.
- Keeps `hasExitWake`: exec notifications, `process poll` guidance and durable adoption use it.
- `protocol:gen`, `ui:validators:gen`, `protocol:gen:swift` and `protocol:gen:kotlin` produce no diff.

Net change: 11 insertions, 358 deletions, 12 files.

## Evidence

Real isolated Gateway from source with its own port and state, real agent (`gpt-6-astra` through the OpenAI Responses API). The agent itself started `sh wait-for-deploy.sh` as a background exec whose exit wakes the chat, then ended its turn. Before: `main` at `5fbdf6989130`. After: this branch. Desktop 1440×900, dark theme. The avatar is blurred.

| State | Before (`main`) | After (this branch) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Idle, waiting on the command | ![Before: Waiting on sh wait-for-deploy.sh card above the composer, desktop dark](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/87b78165-ebf2-4c44-8ce2-9b69ef12bd00) | ![After: no card above the composer, desktop dark](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9763ee4f-475d-4bb0-84b5-87a09e94db3f) |
| Details open | ![Before: Details lists sh wait-for-deploy.sh while the composer card repeats it, desktop dark](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ea2e334b-0c78-4fc5-aac4-e2be8d2a17dc) | ![After: Details lists sh wait-for-deploy.sh and View all processes; no composer card, desktop dark](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/521d2c17-c0a5-4838-8a0d-36efe67a7977) |

- Before: `.chat-waiters` count 1. After: count 0.
- Details → Processes lists `sh wait-for-deploy.sh` and **View all processes** on both sides.
- `sessions.processes.list` on the same running command: before `{status: "running", wakesSession: true, …}`; after `{status: "running", …}` with no `wakesSession`.
- After the command exited on the branch Gateway, the wake turn ran and the agent replied: "The script completed successfully and reported that deployment finished: v2 is live."

Checks:

- `ocx test`: `bash-process-observation.test.ts`, `chat-composer-content.test.tsx`, `chat-composer-status.test.tsx`, `chat-pane-side-panels.test.ts`, `chat-processes-panel.test.ts` pass.
- `tsgo:ui`, `tsgo:core`, scoped oxlint and oxfmt, `lint:ui:styles` (stylelint), `check:control-ui-controllers`, `ui:i18n:verify` pass.
- Control UI budget, `ui:check-performance --base-dist` against the `5fbdf6989130` build:
  - chat boot CSS gzip −112 B (139439 → 139327); total CSS −112 B gzip / −871 B raw.
  - chat boot JS: `control-ui-boot-chat` is 506 B smaller raw, but its hash-normalized gzip is +81 B, so chat boot JS reads +54 B gzip (1310823 → 1310877), inside the 64 B build-variance allowance. `gzip -9` of the same chunk is −127 B. Startup JS −21 B, New Session JS −21 B.
- `ocx build --dts` passes; the packed tarball integrity check, `openclaw --version` and `openclaw gateway --help` from the packed tarball pass.

prs.title: feat(memory): add CJK bigram companion FTS index for two-character queries
prs.body:
Resolves #170997

## What Problem This Solves
When using `store.fts.tokenizer: "trigram"`, SQLite FTS5 requires query terms to be at least 3 characters long. As a result, two-character CJK queries (ubiquitous in Chinese and Japanese, e.g. "設定", "記憶", "台北") cannot be matched by FTS5 and currently fall back to an unranked substring scan. This causes:
1. **Zero BM25 ranking**: Keyword scores contribute 0, leaving result ordering purely arbitrary or vector-dominated.
2. **Slow fallback**: On larger corpora, fallback substring scanning is significantly slower than index-backed lookups (901 ms vs 99 ms on 1,301 chunks).

Because `node:sqlite` does not allow registering custom FTS5 tokenizers at runtime, an in-engine "bigram" tokenizer cannot be added.

This PR adds an opt-in companion Han bigram FTS index (`memory.search.store.fts.cjk: "bigram"`).

### Design
- **Companion Table**: `memory_index_chunks_cjk_fts` uses `tokenize='unicode61'`. Han runs in chunk text are encoded as overlapping character bigrams separated by spaces.
- **Two-Character Query Routing**: Queries consisting of 2-character Han terms bypass the trigram leg and query the companion table directly via `cjkBigramQuery`, providing full BM25 ranking.
- **Mixed OR Recovery**: When searching under `matchAny: true` with mixed Han and short ASCII terms (e.g. `設定 AI`), results are combined across companion BM25 hits and substring candidates via bounded UNION ALL.
- **Non-Regression**: ASCII terms, single-character terms, and queries with 3 or more characters continue using their existing trigram/unicode61 execution paths.
- **Derived State & Lifecycle**:
  - Enabling or disabling `store.fts.cjk: "bigram"` rebuilds only the FTS index leg without requiring any re-embedding. When disabled, `dropDisabledMemoryFts` drops the companion table.
  - Batched writes derive companion rows directly from the write plan using Kysely batch operations without rereading canonical chunks.
  - Deletions via `purgeForgottenMemory` and full resets via `MEMORY_INDEX_DERIVED_TABLES` ensure forgotten chunks are completely expunged from the companion index.
  - Reused schema admissions skip redundant schema scans or DROP queries.
- **Encapsulation & Architecture**: Companion SQL generation is strictly internal to Memory Core (`manager-search-shared.ts`). No implementation SQL builders or table-specific query generators are exported through the public Plugin SDK.

## Evidence

### Benchmarks
Measured on a CJK-heavy corpus (1,301 chunks, 93% with Han text), across 400 two-character terms:
- **Trigram only (baseline)**: Recalled 400/400, BM25-ranked 0/400, 901 ms total (unranked substring fallback)
- **With CJK bigram companion**: Recalled 400/400, BM25-ranked 400/400, 99 ms total (10x faster + BM25 ranked)
- Storage overhead: Companion index adds 0.84 MB alongside the 3.89 MB trigram index.

### Shipped CLI & Gateway Behavior Proof
Demonstrating execution of the shipped `openclaw` CLI binary against a production workspace upgraded from latest stable (`v2026.11.2`) with existing settings, chunks, and embeddings:

#### 1. Binary Version & Environment
```console
$ openclaw --version
OpenClaw 2026.11.2
$ node --version
v26.3.1
$ git rev-parse HEAD
5b9b11183cd58525b5832a8ba71f3a228229f3d9
```

#### 2. Shipped CLI Search Execution (Short Han Query `設定`)
```console
$ openclaw memory search --query "設定"
```

prs.title: fix(cli): invalidate Gateway-cached MCP runtimes on mcp reload
prs.body:
Closes #164642

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw mcp reload` reported "Disposed cached MCP runtimes", but it only disposed CLI-local runtimes. The Gateway process owns its own cached session MCP runtimes, and the CLI command could not reach across the process boundary — so the Gateway's stdio MCP server kept serving the stale runtime and subsequent agent turns never saw the new MCP config.

## What Changed

- New gateway method `mcp.reloadRuntimes` (`mcp-app` family, `operator.write`): disposes the Gateway-side session MCP runtimes via the existing `disposeAllSessionMcpRuntimes` owner.
- The CLI's `mcp reload` dispatches the method before the local dispose and degrades gracefully when no Gateway is reachable (the CLI-local dispose always runs; the log states which side was disposed).

## Evidence

- Handler regression (`mcp.reload-runtimes.test.ts`): the method disposes all session MCP runtimes and acknowledges `{ ok: true }`. Red on `origin/main` (no such method).
- Suites: recovery 222/222, `session-accessor.readonly` 26/26, `server-startup-post-attach` 115/115; `tsc` core clean in all touched files.
- The reporter's source inspection (CLI-local dispose only) matches the pre-fix behavior; the gateway-side dispose reuses the same owner the server-close path already calls.


## Update — 2026-10-04 (Rev 3 rework)

- **Lease-preserving reload**: the handler now runs the Gateway's own config-reload path (`reloadSessionMcpRuntimes`, the same one the hot-reload flow uses) instead of the shutdown-grade `disposeAllSessionMcpRuntimes` — admitted calls keep their runtimes; only stale ones rebuild on the next turn. The manager's `reloadConfig` propagates per-runtime reload failures (no swallowed errors).
- **Authority revalidation**: the handler reads the request's mutation authority and asserts it current immediately before the reload — a caller revoked during the acquisition wait can no longer trigger it.
- **CLI output**: the failure branch now states which side was disposed and that the Gateway-side reload was **not confirmed** (no more misleading "active agents use new config" assurance when the reload did not run); the no-Gateway case is labeled explicitly. The import-boundary assertion follows.
- Handler tests: reload shape (`reloadPlugins: false`), authority revalidation observed, and the failure path responding with an error shape.

Still open: the authority-chain live evidence (allowed reload, read-only rejection, queued revocation preventing closure, discovery/active-call survival) and the command-scope framing — the reload semantics now match the Gateway's own hot-reload behavior rather than a Gateway-wide teardown.


## Update — 2026-11-06 (Rev 5 findings)

- **Unconfirmed cleanup joined into the reload outcome** (`src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime-parts.ts`): a session-parts reload that retires servers now throws when the recorded cleanup failure is outstanding, so a Gateway-level reload cannot resolve successfully while a retired transport's cleanup is unconfirmed. The hot-reload caller already degrades a rejected reload to a warning (`disposeMcpRuntimesWithTimeout`); the RPC path now surfaces it as an error response.
- **Unapplied config reported, not claimed** (`src/gateway/server-methods/mcp-app.ts`, `src/cli/mcp-cli.reload.ts`): the handler response carries `configApplied` next to `reloaded`. With `gateway.reload.mode=off` the command rebuilds runtimes from the published snapshot but leaves pending on-disk edits unapplied, and the CLI prints that caveat instead of promising new config.
- **Discovery order**: `mcp.reloadRuntimes` moved out of the legacy advertised prefix into the additive section (frozen-prefix assertion green again), and `since` follows the protocol guard's current train (`2026.11`).
- **CLI + docs**: the reload command moved to a sibling module (`mcp-cli.reload.ts`) per the line-cap ratchet; `docs/cli/mcp/registry.md` now states that reload contacts the configured Gateway and rebuilds from the published snapshot.
- Regression: `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime-parts.reload-cleanup.test.ts` — a reload whose retired part fails cleanup rejects; red against the prior revision (verified by checkout-swap).

prs.title: fix(dns): publish CoreDNS config atomically so failed writes keep the operator's files
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #184888. `openclaw dns setup --apply` rewrote the operator's existing CoreDNS `Corefile`, the generated `.server` files, and the zone bootstrap through a truncating in-place write: `fs.writeFileSync` directly on the final path, or `sudo tee` (which also truncates) for root-owned paths. An ENOSPC, crash, or kill between truncation and write completion left the operator's CoreDNS configuration empty or partial, with no recovery copy anywhere — the file lives outside OpenClaw's state directory, so OpenClaw held none.

## User Impact

An operator running wide-area discovery DNS setup on a host that already runs CoreDNS could lose their entire CoreDNS configuration to a mid-write failure, breaking LAN-wide DNS resolution until the file was restored by hand. With this change, a failed or interrupted publication leaves the previous `Corefile` byte-for-byte intact, no longer restarts CoreDNS on a failed path, and the command reports the failure instead of silently proceeding.

## Why This Approach

Publication goes through the repo's atomic-write convention (`@openclaw/fs-safe` `replaceFileAtomicSync`): a same-directory staged file + rename, fsynced, parent dir synced. Root-owned paths fall back to a privileged staged publish. The already-safe zone publisher (`replaceWideAreaZoneFile`) is unchanged.

### Review findings, addressed one by one

Round 1 (reviewed head `5b0061eb`):

- **[P2] Resolve file symlinks before invoking the atomic publisher** — fixed. `resolvePublicationTarget` walks the destination's symlink chain (bounded at 32 hops, dangling links included) to the final target before publication, restoring the plain write's follow-the-link semantics while leaving the operator's link in place. A dangling link resolves to its missing target, which the plain write would have created.
- **[P2] Preserve ownership on the ordinary atomic path** — fixed. A rename publishes a new inode, so the staged file receives the operator's uid/gid before it replaces theirs. Setting a group outside the invoking account's memberships fails EPERM, which the publication router treats as a permission failure and re-runs through the privileged path (which chowns under sudo) — privilege is used only when necessary.
- **[P1] Create privileged staging files privately before writing content** — fixed. The privileged path creates the staging sibling exclusive and mode 0600 (`sudo install -m 600 /dev/null`) *before* any configuration byte exists, then `sudo tee`s into that existing private file, applies preserved uid/gid/mode, and renames.
- **[P2] Respect the operator's umask for newly created files** — fixed. Both publishers create fresh files with `0666 & ~process.umask()` (the plain write's contract) instead of a hardcoded 0644.
- **[P2] Narrow the mocked tee destination before writing it** — fixed in `5401ceca`.

Round 2 (reviewed head `5048abb1`):

- **[P1] Keep ordinary staging private until ownership is restored** — fixed in `5503e4e8`. The atomic writer now stages with mode 0600, so the configuration bytes are never readable by an account outside the operator's readership — not even in the window between writing them and publishing them. The operator's uid/gid and final mode are restored on the staged file immediately before the rename. New regression observes the staged file at the ownership hand-off (the moment it holds the bytes) and requires it to still be 0600 there.
- **[P2] Flush privileged staging before publishing it** — fixed in `5503e4e8`: the privileged path flushes the staged file before the rename and the parent directory after it.
- **[P2] Match the actual sudo tee command in the regression** — fixed in `5503e4e8`: the regression matched `" sudo tee "` against a joined command string that never carries that prefix, so the ordering assertion could not hold on any POSIX run. It now matches the structured executable and argument fields.
- **[medium] Verify staging confidentiality across the ownership transition** — the mechanism is fixed in `5503e4e8`, and the macOS run below samples the staged file itself.

Round 3 (reviewed head `5503e4e8`):

- **[P2] Wait for the privileged staging file to finish synchronizing** — fixed in `c6cf53f1`. macOS `sync` ignores pathname operands and only schedules a global sync that may return before the flush completes, so the previous repair did not provide the promised crash-safety on the supported platform. The privileged flush now synchronizes the descriptor explicitly: it opens the staged file (and the parent directory after the rename) and fsyncs it through the same runtime that owns the command, so the rename cannot outrun the flush. The regression asserts the flush happens before the rename and the directory flush after it.

Round 4 (reviewed head `c6cf53f1`):

- **[P1] Preserve existing macOS ACLs before replacing configuration files** — fixed in `63dae340`. macOS carries a per-file access policy beside the mode, and a replacement inode does not inherit it, so restoring uid/gid/mode alone dropped a file-specific denial. The publication now captures the policy entries (`ls -lde`) before replacing the file and restores them on the staged file (`chmod +a`) right before the rename, on both the ordinary and the privileged path. The macOS run below shows the deny entry surviving the publication with the account still denied, and a regression runs the real `chmod +a`/`ls -lde` round-trip on the macOS CI shard.
- **[P2] Match the executable before the eval flag in flush assertions** — fixed in `63dae340`. The regression looked for `["-e", execPath]` while the publisher invokes sudo with `[execPath, "-e", script, path]`, so the assertion could not hold; it now matches the real command, which is why the exact-head CI run failed it.

Round 6 (reviewed head `b54b8b3c`):

- **Findings: none** — the review confirmed the three prior code findings resolved with no remaining introduced defect. The remaining items are proof: the interrupted-restoration case above (run 41296608480, case 7) and the capture-failure regression below.
- **ACL-capture failure** — a regression on the macOS CI shard simulates a failed `/bin/ls -lde` capture and asserts the publication aborts with the operator's file byte-identical, its deny entry still present, and no staging sibling left behind (`aborts the publication when the access policy cannot be captured`).

Round 8 (against the round-7 findings, head `b3b64649`):

- **[P2] The capture-failure regression never exercised the capture failure** — fixed in `b3b64649`. The regression spied on the default `child_process` export, but production imports the named `spawnSync`, which the mock factory routes through its own wrapper, so the injection never reached it. The failure is now injected through `spawnSyncMock` itself, wrapping the existing implementation and returning a correctly shaped failed result for `/bin/ls`.
- **Ordinary-path coverage** — new regression in `b3b64649`: a non-permission failure (ENOSPC) from the atomic publisher aborts the publication **without** routing to the privileged fallback; the operator's file stays untouched, no staging sibling remains, and CoreDNS is not restarted. This is the ordinary path the CLI transcript cannot reach on a root-owned target.
- **Leftover check** — the harness now lists hidden entries (`ls -1A`), so a leftover `.Corefile…` / `.openclaw-dns-config…` sibling is actually detected; the earlier `ls -1` listing silently excluded them.

Round 7 evidence (against the round-6 proof gap, head `b54b8b3c` / `04be35d4`):

- **After interruption, on both publishers** — case 7 covers the privileged publisher and the new case 8 covers the ordinary one: the managed symlink target (published through the ordinary path) was denied by a file-specific ACL and made immutable, so the final rename failed after the restoration completed. The managed target stayed byte-identical, its printed policy entry is unchanged (`user:dnsproofreader deny read`), the excluded account is still refused, no staging sibling survived, and CoreDNS was not restarted.
- **Preventing restart** — cases 2, 7 and 8 assert the failure output never reaches the restart step ("Starting CoreDNS" absent) and the CoreDNS service PID is unchanged across the failure.
- **ACL-capture failure** — covered by the in-process regression on the macOS CI shard (`04be35d4`): a failed `/bin/ls -lde` capture aborts the publication with the operator's file byte-identical, its deny entry present, and no staging sibling. An external CLI-level capture failure is not constructible on a healthy host because production pins the system `/bin/ls` precisely so user-installed ls builds cannot enter this path.
- **Through restoration** — the restoration runs entirely inside the staged file's private 0600 mode (chown → chmod +a → grant mode), which is the ordering fix from `b54b8b3c`; the in-process boundary test observes the staged file at that transition on the macOS CI shard, and the external samples of the staged file (mode 600, reader denied) bracket it.

### Data-model compatibility

This change touches no config, state, or database schema. The compatibility surface is the operator's on-disk CoreDNS configuration, and it is pinned by regressions (mode, ownership, symlink, dangling link, umask) and by the macOS run below: a configuration published by the latest stable release keeps its contents, ownership, permissions and symlink after the upgrade to this build.

## Evidence

### Real macOS behavior proof (run)

A macOS-14 runner drove the shipped CLI (`pnpm openclaw dns setup --domain openclaw.internal --apply`) as an unprivileged account against a root-owned, group-restricted `Corefile`, so the privileged staged publication ran with real sudo. An independent local account (`dnsproofreader`, outside the operator's group) stood in for the unauthorized reader. (harness: `proof/macos-dns-publication-proof.sh`, fork branch `proof/macos-dns-publication`)

```
=== case 1: successful privileged publication ===
after publication: mode=640 owner=root:staff; reader denied
=== case 2: a failed privileged publication preserves the operator's Corefile ===
failed publication exit status: 1
Reason: sudo install -m 600 /dev/null /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/.Corefile.openclaw-15596.tmp failed: install: ...: Operation not permitted
operator Corefile after the failed publication: unchanged (.:53 {|  errors|  log|}|# marker-before-interruption|)
=== case 6: an ACL-denied principal stays denied across the publication ===
policy before the publication:
 0: user:dnsproofreader deny read
reader denied before the publication
 0: user:dnsproofreader deny read
reader denied after the publication
=== case 7: an interrupted publication preserves the operator's file and policy ===
interrupted publication exit status: 1
Reason: sudo mv /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/.Corefile.openclaw-9268.tmp /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/Corefile failed: exit 1
operator Corefile after the interrupted publication: unchanged
reader still denied the operator's Corefile
no staging sibling survived
=== case 8: an interrupted ordinary publication preserves the managed target and policy ===
Reason: sudo mv /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/.managed-Corefile.openclaw-9535.tmp /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/managed-Corefile failed: exit 1
managed target after the interruption: unchanged; policy: user:dnsproofreader deny read
reader still denied the managed target
no staging sibling survived; CoreDNS not restarted
=== case 2 restart assertion ===
CoreDNS not restarted across the failed publication (service PID unchanged)
=== case 3: symlinked Corefile keeps its link ===
link preserved: managed-Corefile; managed target updated
=== case 4: latest stable configuration survives the upgrade ===
latest stable exit status: 0
after the upgrade: mode=640 owner=root:staff content=ok
=== PROOF PASSED ===
```

Runs: <https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41296608480> (cases 1-4, 6-7), <https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41297533034> (case 8 ordinary-publisher interruption and the restart-suppression assertions), and <https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41313384334> (the same suite with the leftover check covering hidden staging files). Case 7 fails the final rename after the restoration completed (immutable Corefile), which exercises the interruption point that matters: the operator's file stays byte-identical, its deny entry is still printed, the excluded account is still refused, and the CLI cleaned its staging sibling.

What that establishes, on the supported platform:

- The publication succeeds end to end and the operator's file keeps its **contents, mode (0640) and owner (root:staff)**; the group-excluded account still cannot read it.
- A **failed** privileged publication exits non-zero with the cause (`sudo install ... Operation not permitted`) and leaves the operator's Corefile **byte-identical** with its mode and ownership untouched — the interruption case.
- A **file-specific deny ACL** (`user:dnsproofreader deny read`, not expressible in the mode) survives the publication and the account remains denied — before and after. This is the access-policy preservation that `63dae340` adds.
- A **symlinked** Corefile keeps its link and the managed target is updated instead.
- The configuration published by the **latest stable release** (`openclaw@latest`) still loads and keeps its contents, ownership and permissions after the upgrade to this build.

**The staging window** (the configuration bytes sitting in the sibling file before the rename) is milliseconds long in the real command and cannot be sampled reliably from outside the process — eleven harness iterations established that empirically (PATH interception, NODE_OPTIONS preload, and directory-permission forcing each failed to yield a deterministic sample). That window is therefore covered where it is deterministically observable: the in-process boundary tests run on this PR's macOS CI shard against the real fs and the real fs-safe publisher — `keeps the staged configuration private until the operator's mode is restored` observes the staged file at the ownership hand-off (the moment it holds the bytes) and requires it to still be 0600, and `keeps the operator's macOS access policy across a publication` runs the real `chmod +a`/`ls -lde` policy round-trip through the publication. An earlier run of the external harness did sample the staged file live at `mode=600` with the unauthorized reader denied (<https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41172290366>); the deterministic coverage is the CI shard.

### Regression suite

- Red on base / green on fix: on `main`, an injected ENOSPC during Corefile publication left the Corefile truncated mid-import-line (the issue's damage scenario); with the fix the previous bytes survive and CoreDNS is not restarted.
- POSIX regressions (this PR's CI ubuntu + macOS shards): mode preservation (0640 stays 0640), private staging until the ownership hand-off, macOS access-policy round-trip, symlinked-Corefile publication to the managed target, dangling-link target creation, and the forced-privileged-path publication.
- Windows host note: the development host cannot execute the POSIX-only regressions locally — Windows has no POSIX mode semantics, so the atomic writer's staged-file chmod fails with EPERM and the command routes to the privileged path on this host, and NTFS drops the group/other bits the mode assertions check. Those regressions are verified in this PR's CI; the platform-neutral suite passes locally (10 passed, 11 POSIX/darwin-skipped).
- Checks: `pnpm vitest run src/cli/dns-cli.test.ts src/infra/widearea-dns.test.ts src/infra/widearea-dns.boundary.test.ts`, `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, `tsgo:core`, the cli test-typecheck config, and both ratchets — all clean locally; the full matrix runs in CI.

### Latest head (`5bf22fcb7e`)

Three independent reviews of the publication path (not the hosted bot) found defects that are fixed on this head, and the test mock had drifted from the production contract it stood in for:

The head also merges `origin/main`: the test-line ratchet measures a pull request's merge tree against its merge base, and this branch's base was six days old, so main's own test-line drift was charged to this change. With main merged the lane measures this change alone (`Test lines OK: 6623658; ceiling: 6623949; slack: 291`) and the allocation still covers exactly this change's measured growth. The scalar reconciliation that drift had motivated (#194489) is no longer needed and was closed with its measurement: at `origin/main` (`28b82d78e1`) the tree is 292 lines under its ceiling.

- The privileged inspection replayed the inherited entries at the **parent directory's** ACL indexes; the restore inserts at the recorded position, so those indexes do not exist on the staged file — the publication aborted instead of restoring the policy. The entries are renumbered contiguously now, like the unprivileged reader.
- Stripping the inheritance flags left the separating comma on the entry (`group:admin deny write,`), which is not a valid access policy — any directory with a `file_inherit` grant failed to restore. The separator goes with the flags now.
- The inspection treated every stat failure as a missing destination and continued past a symlink chain it could not resolve; only `ENOENT` is a first creation now, and an unresolved chain aborts.
- The privileged helper scripts ran `process.execPath`, which in the standalone build is the OpenClaw executable itself: it cannot evaluate a script, so the privileged publication failed there and the CLI was briefly run as root. A Node or Bun runtime is resolved now, and the scripts read their path from the last argument.
- The mock re-implemented the inspection script and returned bare strings where the script returns `{ position, entry }` records, so the privileged policy restore was never exercised. The mock now runs the production script, which pins the contract instead of imitating it.

New regressions on this head: the inspection script reports positional records with the inherited entries renumbered; the privileged publication hands the staged file the operator's captured ids before the rename; a failing privileged publication (`sudo mv`) leaves the operator's file byte-identical, removes the staging sibling and does not restart CoreDNS; and the access-policy **order** survives a replacement — the same entries at the same positions, which is what `chmod +a#` exists for (`chmod +a` canonicalizes the order and can put an allow in front of a deny).

### Accepted edge cases

- The staging file's name carries a random component, so another account that may write the destination directory cannot place a file at a known staging path before the privileged steps run. An account that may write that directory can still substitute the staged file between the privileged steps; the operator's directory permissions are the boundary there, and the truncating write this replaces exposed the destination path itself, so the substitution was easier to arrange before, not harder.
- The privileged runtime stays the operator's own toolchain. An account that can replace that runtime could already run it with sudo; the publication does not add a new privilege to it.
- The macOS proof harness runs on this fork's macOS Actions quota, which is currently exhausted (the dispatch on this head was cancelled with zero steps). The macOS regressions therefore run in this PR's upstream macOS CI lane, which executes `src/cli/dns-cli.test.ts` on a macOS runner.

prs.body:
Supersedes #199424 after resolving its conflict with current main.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes enabled tool-output reducers silently being skipped in headless runs and nested Code Mode tool calls.

## User Impact

Enabled middleware such as Tokenjuice can transform actual tool results before they reach the agent, including nested Code Mode shell calls. Exact file/schema results and the surrounding JavaScript envelope retain their existing contracts. Bounded-command guidance recommends the existing terminal-result collection path instead of avoidable short-yield/poll cycles.

No new configuration, dependencies, permission changes, or migrations. Native Codex shell results remain outside this replacement path. This PR does not claim a whole-task token-savings percentage.

## Why This Change Was Made

Headless runs prepare a scoped plugin generation, but middleware discovery consulted the process-global registry. Discovery now follows the current context and its prepared lazy-load inputs. Native catalog calls apply the existing middleware once before guest serialization, using the policy-adjusted arguments actually executed.

Prompt/docs recommend the existing `awaitResults` behavior for bounded commands and distinguish native replacement, CLI wrapping, failure preservation and complete-task measurement. A CI-exposed capacity-test fixture also now accepts the same process record from running or completed retention; all original assertions remain intact.

## Evidence

- Scoped-only, empty-root and same-ID lazy-owner regressions fail on the unchanged base and pass with the fix. The real-worker Code Mode regression covers once-only transformation, executed command/cwd, failure metadata, exact file/schema bytes and the outer envelope.
- Original combined candidate: 43 tests across six files/four shards and full `pnpm build` passed. The build emitted unrelated UI size-budget advisories.
- Built real-model direct and Code Mode probes before conflict integration: synthetic inventory output was reduced from 5,647 to 470 delivered characters including the notice; exit 7/sentinel and exact file/schema results were preserved. No manual CLI wrapper or global-registry workaround. This is boundary proof, not a matched whole-task benchmark.
- Local autoreview of the full original patch (base `520f18975936d49ffc1cf8d02bbd98c4b7981c14`, committed as `4aad990fc6fbdd5ce204fd4d33b99932525220c1`) found no actionable P0–P2 issues. Local ClawSweeper was unavailable; the initial hosted review was queued. These are source-review results, not reviewer-executed tests.
- Conflict integration with main `3c6bb67f82aec52a12644933434a9d5ed7e6ed01` preserves the renamed prompt variable and current background guidance. Middleware production files and regression fixtures remain byte-identical to the original reviewed patch. Post-integration: 89 tests across five files/three shards, scoped lint/types, formatting, MDX and diff checks passed.
- [CI run 43676766068](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43676766068) exposed a running-only lookup in `code-mode.catalog-lifetime.test.ts:76`. `pnpm test:ci-failed 199434 --run` reproduced the original failure locally. No sleeps, retries, longer timeouts or weaker assertions were added. CI's original failing case took 3.326 seconds.

prs.title: fix(agents): retract running deferred dispatcher when nested target starts
prs.body:
Fixes #194168

## What Problem This Solves

Discord progress mode with `toolProgress: true` renders **two identical rows** for each deferred tool call while it runs: one for the `dispatch_action` dispatcher and one for its nested target. Both rows share the same label and `running` status at the same time, even though the transcript records a single execution. This fix retracts the dispatcher row as soon as its nested target starts, so the live draft shows exactly one row per tool call. Independent tool calls with identical labels remain separate.

## Problem

With Discord progress mode and `toolProgress: true`, a deferred tool call dispatched through `dispatch_action` renders as **two identical rows** in the live draft while it runs: one for the dispatcher and one for its nested target. Both rows show the same label and the same `running` status at the same time.

The transcript shows each tool call executed exactly once.

## Root cause

`dispatch_action` is a pure forwarding wrapper. It publishes its own visible prepared item (`tool:<dispatcher-call-id>`) when it starts, and its nested target (`tool_call:<parent>:<name>:<seq>`, `parentToolCallId` = dispatcher id) publishes a second visible item with an identical label. The existing wrapper suppression (`resolveCompletedActivityWrappers` / `finalizeToolActivity`) only collapses a completed wrapper **at run termination**, so while the target is still running both rows stay on the draft.

## Fix

Represent a deferred dispatcher and its nested target as one live operation at the producer (`src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.start.ts`):

- When a nested target starts (`lifecycleProvenance: "nested"`) **with a visible activity**, look up its parent dispatcher from the tracked tool starts.
- If the parent is a `dispatch_action` wrapper that is still visible, retract its row by emitting an `update` item event with `hideFromChannelProgress: true` (the channel progress compositor clears the row by item id).
- Persist `hideFromChannelProgress` on the parent's start record so the dispatcher's terminal event stays hidden too — the run-termination collapse in `finalizeToolActivity` is unchanged.

A nested target whose activity is hidden (for example a routine `progress_card`, or a `wait`/`process.poll` child) does **not** replace the dispatcher: the shared activity owner (`resolveCompletedActivityWrappers`) keeps a wrapper visible when none of its children contributes a visible row, so the dispatcher stays visible until terminal collapse. This matches the routine-wrapper preservation policy established in #165358 and avoids leaving neither the dispatcher nor a hidden routine target countable.

A `dispatch_action` that fails to dispatch (no nested target) keeps its own visible row with the error, so no information is lost. Independent tool calls with identical labels stay separate because they have no parent/child relationship.

## Evidence

### Regressions (each fails on the prior head, passes with the fix)

1. `retracts a running deferred dispatcher once its nested target starts` — a visible `web_search` target replaces the running dispatcher row.
   - Before: the dispatcher receives no retraction update → assertion `expected [] to have a length of 1` fails.
   - After: exactly one `phase: "update"` item event with `hideFromChannelProgress: true`, and the target row stays visible.

2. `keeps a running deferred dispatcher when its nested target is routine` — a `progress_card` target (hidden activity) does not replace the dispatcher.
   - Before: the dispatcher is retracted anyway → assertion `expected [ { itemId: 'tool:dispatcher', ... } ] to have a length of +0 but got 1` fails.
   - After: no retraction update is emitted and the dispatcher stays visible.

```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  15 passed (15)
```

### Related suites (all pass)

- `src/infra/agent-activity-events.test.ts` — 25 passed
- `src/channels/progress-draft-compositor.test.ts` — 59 passed
- `extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.draft-preview.rest.test.ts` — 16 passed

### CI-equivalent checks

- `oxlint --type-aware --deny=warn` — clean
- `node scripts/run-format.mts --check` — clean
- `check-test-lines-ratchet` — pass (new test lines covered by `config/test-lines-allocations/issue-194168-deferred-dispatcher.txt`, 87)
- `check-test-mock-exports --prune` — 6387 → 6387, no new violations
- typecheck on changed files — 0 errors

## What was not tested

No live Discord round trip was run in this environment. The regression exercises the producer event stream (`handleToolExecutionStart`), which is the source both channels and the Control UI consume; the Discord draft-preview test suite confirms the retraction path (`hideFromChannelProgress` + item id) is honored by the compositor.

prs.title: fix(cli): cancel interrupted gateway secret reads
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw security audit` (and the other commands that resolve command-scoped secrets through the Gateway: `qr`, `directory …`) kept working for up to 30s after Ctrl-C when the Gateway was slow to answer `secrets.resolve`, then printed a `[secrets] … gateway secrets.resolve unavailable` diagnostic and finished local secret resolution and the command body while the CLI was already stopping.

## User Impact

Interrupting that read now exits in ~1.7s instead of ~43.5s on the same harness, with no post-interrupt `[secrets]` diagnostic and no command output after the interruption notice. Nothing changes when the read is not interrupted: the same 30s timeout still falls back locally with the identical diagnostic and report (controls below).

## Why This Change Was Made

`secrets.resolve` is a read — there is nothing to settle after an interrupt — so it only needed to join the CLI's existing cancellation contract:

- `src/cli/command-secret-gateway.ts:168` forwards the command's ambient signal (`getAsyncWorkSignal()`) into the request; `callGateway` already supports it.
- `src/cli/command-secret-gateway.ts:541` stops before the local fallback when that read was cancelled.

Precedent in the same family: #199307 (merged — gateway call reads), #199353 (state-store guard reads).

Classification: **behavior-completing** (interrupted path only). The cancelled read is rethrown rather than swallowed, so the command never starts and the existing top-level failure path prints its usual `The CLI command failed.` / doctor lines — the same shape accepted in #199353.

## Evidence

Harness: a synthetic loopback WebSocket peer speaks the real wire protocol (`connect.challenge` → `connect` → `hello-ok`, protocol 4, `operator.admin`) and answers every request except `secrets.resolve`, which it holds. The CLI runs under a real PTY (`script -qfec … src/entry.ts security audit`) with an isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME` / `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` / `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, `gateway.auth.token` as an environment SecretRef (one of the security-audit command targets), and an ephemeral port. SIGINT goes to the recorded CLI pid 300ms after the `secrets.resolve` request is observed (`msFromReadToSigint` 303 / 302 ms). BASE is the pristine tree at this branch's base `99157f8f8c4e`; HEAD is `9e1803590f7f`; both ran the same harness bytes.

| Run | Interrupt | `secrets.resolve` | Exit | `[secrets] … unavailable` | Audit report | Socket closed after SIGINT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BASE | yes | held | 130 | yes (42.7s after SIGINT) | yes | 29672 ms |
| HEAD | yes | held | 130 | no | no | **8 ms** |
| BASE control | no | held | 0 | yes | yes | — |
| HEAD control | no | held | 0 | yes (identical text) | yes | — |
| BASE control | no | answered | 0 | no | yes | — |
| HEAD control | no | answered | 0 | no | yes | — |

SIGINT → exit: BASE **43467 ms**, HEAD **1737 ms**. The residual ~1.7s is the CLI's existing failure/cleanup path, not a gateway wait; the held read itself ends 8 ms after the interrupt on HEAD.

Focused regression (remote container, Node 24.22.1, same test files, only production reverted for BASE):

```text
BASE:   2 failed | 23 passed
        - forwards this command's interrupt signal to the gateway secret read
        - stops an interrupted gateway secret read before local exec resolution
HEAD:   25 passed
```

BASE's failure is the shape being fixed: the interrupted call resolves through the local fallback, and the recorded diagnostic even embeds the swallowed invariant error — `memory status: gateway secrets.resolve unavailable (expected undefined to be AbortSignal …); resolved command secrets locally.` The second test also shows an `exec` SecretRef provider does not run after the interruption (its marker file stays absent).

Consumers of the changed module in the same container: `command-config-resolution.test.ts`, `qr-cli.test.ts`, `security-cli.test.ts`, `command-secret-gateway.memory-headers.test.ts` → **38 passed**.

Mechanical gates: `check:test-mock-exports` OK (6319 grandfathered factories), `check:test-lines-ratchet` OK (+33, allowance 400), `check:line-cap-ratchet` OK, touched-file `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` clean.

### Not tested

- SIGTERM (same atomic close path, only SIGINT measured).
- `qr` and `directory` were not driven end to end; they call this same read.
- No packed/dist build for this change: the PTY runs use the source entry via `tsx`, and unit/consumer tiers ran in a container.
- The startup banner tagline is random per run, not a behavior difference.

### Cleanup

Each run used a fresh `mkdtemp` state/config root, an ephemeral loopback port, and terminated the synthetic peer. No production Gateway, session, token, or config file was touched.

prs.title: fix(android): match Control UI page scheme to the gateway socket
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A discovered gateway on a non-loopback address opens a TLS socket even when its Bonjour record omits `gatewayTls`. The Android Control UI page did not use that decision. It chose `http` or `https` only from `endpoint.tlsEnabled`, so the page stayed on cleartext while the socket was TLS.

The Terminal, dashboard, and desktop screens load that page after the operator session connects. The page origin is where the signing bridge answers a challenge. A cleartext page is the wrong origin for a connection the socket policy already refused to leave on cleartext.

Manual LAN cleartext is unchanged. A stored pin still does not upgrade that page to HTTPS, matching the socket. A manual remote host whose cleartext toggle is off stays on HTTPS, also matching the socket.

## Evidence

API 34 emulator, play debug build, head `8f4143070ae`. The production `ControlUiWebView` loaded a page on the emulator's private LAN address `10.0.2.15`. The discovered endpoint had `tlsEnabled` false and no advertised fingerprint. The manual endpoint used the cleartext toggle.

```console
$ adb -s emulator-5554 shell am instrument -w -r -e class ai.openclaw.app.ui.ControlUiSchemeDeviceTest ai.openclaw.app.debug.test/androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner
OK (2 tests)

url=https://10.0.2.15:36997
page=https://10.0.2.15:36997/ wss://10.0.2.15:36997 NATIVE_AUTH

url=http://10.0.2.15:34079
page=http://10.0.2.15:34079/ ws://10.0.2.15:34079 NATIVE_AUTH
```

![Discovered LAN page loaded over HTTPS and installed native auth](https://github.com/SebTardif/openclaw/raw/8f4143070ae6055df10f80e3928f0451d0d38978/apps/android/app/src/androidTest/proof/https-discovered.png)

![Manual LAN cleartext page stayed on HTTP](https://github.com/SebTardif/openclaw/raw/8f4143070ae6055df10f80e3928f0451d0d38978/apps/android/app/src/androidTest/proof/http-manual-lan.png)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** The Control UI WebView origin follows the socket. A discovered private-LAN host with no gatewayTls advertisement loads HTTPS, and the native auth bridge publishes a wss gateway URL. Manual private-LAN cleartext stays HTTP and publishes a ws URL.
- **Real environment tested:** Android emulator API 34 google_apis arm64, play debug app `ai.openclaw.app.debug`, head `8f4143070ae`. The page host is the emulator guest address 10.0.2.15.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Installed the play debug apk and ran `adb -s emulator-5554 shell am instrument -w -r -e class ai.openclaw.app.ui.ControlUiSchemeDeviceTest ai.openclaw.app.debug.test/androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner`.
- **Evidence after fix:** The WebView document and the screenshots above. Discovered LAN showed `https://10.0.2.15:36997/` plus `wss://10.0.2.15:36997` and `NATIVE_AUTH`. Manual LAN showed `http://10.0.2.15:34079/` plus `ws://10.0.2.15:34079` and `NATIVE_AUTH`.
- **Observed result after fix:** The production WebView loaded the HTTPS page for the discovered case and the HTTP page for manual cleartext. Both documents received the native auth payload for that origin.
- **What was not tested:** A physical phone. This was not a full OpenClaw gateway login. The page is a local document served to the production WebView so the loaded scheme and the installed auth bridge are visible.

## Summary

The page URL is built from the same TLS decision as the gateway socket. No changelog entry.

```python
"""Exercise ClawHub credential diagnostics through the normal built public CLI."""
import argparse
import hashlib
import http.server
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import signal
import subprocess
import tempfile
import threading
import time


def run_cli(command, checkout, env):
    child = subprocess.Popen(command, cwd=checkout, env=env, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, start_new_session=True)
    try:
        stdout, stderr = child.communicate(timeout=30)
    except BaseException:
        if child.poll() is None:
            os.killpg(child.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
        child.communicate()
        raise
    return child.returncode, stdout, stderr


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("checkout", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("phase", choices=["base", "head"])
    parser.add_argument("node", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    checkout = args.checkout.resolve()
    head = subprocess.check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"], cwd=checkout, text=True).strip()
    assert not subprocess.check_output(["git", "status", "--porcelain"], cwd=checkout), "Proof requires a clean committed checkout"
    build = json.loads((checkout / "dist/build-info.json").read_text())
    stamp = json.loads((checkout / "dist/.buildstamp").read_text())
    assert build["commit"] == head and stamp["inputsClean"], "Proof requires the clean normal build of this commit"
    started = time.monotonic()
    token = "fixture-K83-ordinary-secret"
    marker = "SAFE_CLAWHUB_OPERATOR_MARKER"
    cases = [
        ("config-query-json", "config", False, True, "reflection"),
        ("env-trending-json", "env", True, True, "reflection"),
        ("legacy-env-query-text", "legacy-env", False, False, "reflection"),
        ("ordinary-error", "config", False, True, "ordinary-error"),
        ("authenticated-success", "config", False, True, "success"),
        ("anonymous-success", "anonymous", False, True, "success"),
    ]
    records = []
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="clawhub-token-proof-", dir=args.output.resolve().parent) as temporary:
        root = Path(temporary)
        config = root / "openclaw.json"
        config.write_text("{}\n")
        auth = root / "clawhub.json"
        base_env = {key: value for key, value in os.environ.items() if not key.startswith(("OPENCLAW_", "CLAWHUB_", "CLAWDHUB_")) and key not in {"GH_TOKEN", "GITHUB_TOKEN"}}
        base_env.update({"HOME": str(root), "XDG_CONFIG_HOME": str(root / "xdg"), "OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR": str(root / "state"), "OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH": str(config), "CLAWHUB_CONFIG_PATH": str(auth), "NO_COLOR": "1", "PATH": str(args.node.parent) + os.pathsep + base_env.get("PATH", "")})
        cli = [str(args.node), str(checkout / "openclaw.mjs"), "skills", "search"]
        help_status, help_stdout, help_stderr = run_cli(cli + ["--help"], checkout, base_env)
        assert help_status == 0 and "--json" in help_stdout, help_stderr
        for name, source, trending, json_mode, mode in cases:
            env = dict(base_env)
            auth.write_text(json.dumps({"token": token if source == "config" else "fixture-config-not-selected"}))
            if source == "env":
                env["CLAWHUB_TOKEN"] = token
                env["CLAWHUB_AUTH_TOKEN"] = "fixture-legacy-env-not-selected"
            elif source == "legacy-env":
                env["CLAWHUB_TOKEN"] = " "
                env["CLAWHUB_AUTH_TOKEN"] = token
            elif source == "anonymous":
                auth.write_text("{}\n")
            before = {p.name: hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() for p in [config, auth]}
            received = []

            class Peer(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
                def do_GET(self):
                    authorization = self.headers.get("Authorization")
                    received.append({"path": self.path, "authorizationPresent": authorization is not None, "authorizationMatchesSentinel": authorization == "Bearer " + token})
                    if mode == "success":
                        text = json.dumps({"results": [{"score": 0.9, "slug": "fixture-result", "displayName": "Fixture Result", "summary": "SAFE_RESULT_TEXT", "source": "clawhub", "ownerHandle": "fixture-owner", "version": "1.2.3"}]})
                    else:
                        text = marker + (" refused " + token if mode == "reflection" else " ordinary upstream failure")
                    body = text.encode()
                    self.send_response(200 if mode == "success" else 400)
                    self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json" if mode == "success" else "text/plain")
                    self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
                    self.send_header("Connection", "close")
                    self.end_headers()
                    self.wfile.write(body)

                def log_message(self, *_args):
                    pass

            peer = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Peer)
            thread = threading.Thread(target=peer.serve_forever, daemon=True)
            thread.start()
            env["OPENCLAW_CLAWHUB_URL"] = "http://127.0.0.1:" + str(peer.server_address[1])
            command = cli + ([] if trending else ["fixture-redaction"]) + (["--json"] if json_mode else [])
            at = time.monotonic()
            try:
                status, stdout, stderr = run_cli(command, checkout, env)
            finally:
                peer.shutdown()
                peer.server_close()
                thread.join(timeout=5)
                assert not thread.is_alive(), "Peer cleanup did not finish"
            assert len(received) == 1, received
            assert received[0]["authorizationMatchesSentinel"] == (source != "anonymous"), received
            assert received[0]["authorizationPresent"] == (source != "anonymous"), received
            expected_path = "/api/v1/trending?kind=skills&limit=20" if trending else "/api/v1/search?q=fixture-redaction"
            assert received[0]["path"] == expected_path, received
            output = stdout + stderr
            if mode == "success":
                assert status == 0 and stderr == "", (status, stderr)
                result = json.loads(stdout)["results"]
                assert len(result) == 1 and result[0]["slug"] == "fixture-result" and result[0]["summary"] == "SAFE_RESULT_TEXT", result
            else:
                assert status == 1 and marker in output and "400" in output, (status, output)
                if json_mode:
                    failure = json.loads(stdout)
                    assert failure["ok"] is False and failure["error"]["type"] == "cli_error", failure
                else:
                    assert stdout == "" and marker in stderr, (stdout, stderr)
            present = token in output
            assert present == (mode == "reflection" and args.phase == "base"), (name, args.phase, "Unexpected credential-presence observation")
            after = {p.name: hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() for p in [config, auth]}
            assert before == after, "Configuration/credential bytes changed"
            records.append({"case": name, "source": source, "mode": mode, "trending": trending, "json": json_mode, "command": command, "status": status, "requests": received, "stdout": stdout, "stderr": stderr, "sentinelPresent": present, "safeMarkerPresent": marker in output, "configAndCredentialBytesUnchanged": before == after, "elapsedMs": round((time.monotonic() - at) * 1000)})
    receipt = {"phase": args.phase, "head": head, "at": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime()), "buildInfo": build, "inputsClean": stamp["inputsClean"], "collectorSha256": hashlib.sha256(Path(__file__).read_bytes()).hexdigest(), "helpStatus": help_status, "records": records, "cleanup": "all children completed without timeout; all peers closed/joined; temporary HOME/config/state removed", "elapsedMs": round((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000)}
    args.output.write_text(json.dumps(receipt, indent=2))
    print(json.dumps({"output": str(args.output), "phase": args.phase, "head": head, "cases": len(records), "collectorSha256": receipt["collectorSha256"], "elapsedMs": receipt["elapsedMs"]}))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

prs.title: docs(release): document npm trusted publisher management
prs.body:
## Problem

OpenClaw's release recovery runbook did not give operators the supported npm commands or exact binding needed to audit, create, replace, or revoke plugin trusted publishers.

## Change

- document npm 11.15+ prerequisites and the pinned `pnpm exec npm` route
- add exact `npm trust list`, `npm trust github`, and ID-scoped `npm trust revoke` commands
- bind GitHub repository, workflow filename, environment, and direct-publish permission to the current plugin workflow
- preserve first-package bootstrap, two-day initial-publication expiry, read-only OIDC preflight, and no-token-fallback boundaries

## Validation

- `pnpm exec npm --version` → 12.2.1
- `pnpm exec npm trust list --help`
- `pnpm exec npm trust github --help`
- `pnpm exec npm trust revoke --help`
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check .agents/skills/release-openclaw-maintainer/references/publication-recovery.md`
- `git diff --check`
- existing focused workflow suite: 64 tests passed before the final docs-only revision
- independent GPT-6.1 Sol P0–P2 review: clean after resolving one stale CLI-availability finding

Implements RRI-501.

prs.title: fix(logbook): clear obsolete errors when retrying actions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Logbook retains an earlier failure while showing a successful Ask or Daily standup retry.

## User Impact

Retrying an action removes its obsolete failure without hiding an independent timeline-read error. Questions and expanded activity details remain intact.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing Logbook owner records which operation owns its single error and retires only the retried operation’s feedback. Request admission, permissions, capture behavior, and durable state are unchanged. The existing single-error, last-writer presentation remains unchanged.

prs.title: fix(knowledge): Scribe controls hide cancellation and removal
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Scribe controls implying that cancelled work can resume and obscuring the difference between disabling an automation and removing it.

## User Impact

Scribes now offer **Disable**, **Stop and disable** for an enabled running automation, and **Enable**. Disabled status and outcome messages use the same terminology. **Remove automation…** names the separate deletion action and preserves the conversation. Its confirmation describes cancellation as a request, not an already completed stop.

The longer controls wrap within narrow screens instead of clipping. Scheduling, cancellation, permission checks, revision checks, and retained history are unchanged; **Run now** remains an explicit override for a disabled automation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing update owner persists `enabled: false` and cancels active work. Re-enabling does not resume the cancelled occurrence. The removal owner deletes the automation and requests cancellation separately. The view now describes those existing operations, without adding state or changing requests.

A one-line width bound lets the existing wrapping layout work with the longer action labels. No new styles, controls, or recovery flow are introduced beyond that bound and the presentation copy.

## Evidence

- **51 focused checks passed:** 30 Scribe-view cases, 16 Scribe-state cases, three disable/ownership-cancellation cases, and two real scheduler removal/disable receipt cases. The idle/running control regressions fail on main for the old labels and pass after correction.
- The real scheduler test now verifies that re-enabling leaves the original abort signal cancelled and does not invoke the runner again. An explicit later run is a new invocation. Separate existing owner tests verify abort and terminal records for removal and disablement.
- Actual-component browser flow covers running → disable → enable → remove confirmation, Cancel, and confirmed removal. It sends exactly two revision-bound `cron.update` requests and one `cron.remove`, with no extra run or chat request. Synthetic Gateway responses and runner edges only; no live Scribe, Knowledge store, or account was changed.
- Desktop and 400-pixel emulated-phone captures were inspected. The longer labels initially overflowed to 483.8px; the scoped width bound keeps all controls within 400px and retains the existing wrap. This is the production component/styles in an isolated minimal host, not the full app shell or native-device proof.
- Scoped TypeScript lint, plugin/core-test typechecks, formatting, i18n verification and diff checks pass. **Direct stylesheet lint remains red with the same 30 pre-existing diagnostics on main and the patched file**, compared by rule/text/column; no diagnostic was added, limit raised, or unrelated CSS changed.
- Measured checks: view/state group 3.14s; disable/enable owner file 39.11s including cold worker compilation (newly extended case 799ms); two removal/disable cases 39.27s including compilation (tests 841ms total). Remote CI and its timings are pending.
- Simplification: net three production lines (two formatting-expanded copy lines and one CSS bound), 29 test lines, and no net documentation growth. Internal state enums and existing helper contracts remain unchanged.

Before is verified main `bcfa6ca00c18fcc619aa1dbf3de301aceec0cd95`. Main through `18a62d6ff93428f15b0801ba5efe4ef0452a8f15` has no affected owner/presentation drift. This independent PR complements [#199163](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199163) and [#199259](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199259). Related [#195010](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/195010) internationalizes the old Pause/Resume copy rather than correcting these effects.

Knowledge → Scribes → open the ongoing scribe. Matched 1030×420 crops from the actual component at 1100×820, light theme, with synthetic data.

prs.title: fix(codex): keep Model Setup probes out of chat history
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When OpenClaw shares its Codex home with Codex Desktop or the CLI, a tool-free Model Setup probe can appear in chat history. If a user reopens that thread and asks it to run a command, the probe's saved instructions can still cause a tool refusal.

## User Impact

New Model Setup probes use temporary Codex threads and stay out of saved chat history.

## Why This Change Was Made

Model Setup creates keys in the `setup-inference:incognito-…` namespace. Add that namespace to the shared incognito key classifier so the existing Codex `thread/start` logic sends `ephemeral: true`. The setup turn still runs with `disableTools: true`.

The regression test covers a probe-shaped key and an ordinary key in the same namespace.

## Evidence

### Focused regression on upstream main

On `3c6bb67f8`, the probe-key case failed against the original classifier. With the patch, all 10 cases passed.

```sh
pnpm test:unit:fast src/shared/incognito-session-key.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

### Live verification on OpenClaw 2026.11.3

- Built the equivalent release patch from source on macOS and ran the same focused suite. All 10 tests passed.
- A real Model Setup probe using the installed Codex app-server completed successfully. The captured `thread/start` request included `ephemeral: true`. After the probe app-server exited, the matching rollout file count and SQLite thread row count were both zero.
- After restarting OpenClaw with the patch, a fresh ordinary chat executed `pwd` through the shell tool and produced a normal rollout. Configuration and existing chat history matched their pre-deployment fingerprints.

prs.title: fix(openai): conversations fail when hooks override saved-context replay
prs.body:
Related: #198357

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes OpenAI conversations failing with a saved-context conflict when a later payload hook overrides checkpoint replay settings, and restores the recovery guidance that was lost on the way to chat.

## User Impact

Conversations using retained OpenAI checkpoints keep their context without re-storing conflicting checkpoint records. If an item conflict still occurs, the chat shows the existing recovery instructions instead of only the raw provider error. No configuration changes, migrations, transcript rewrites, or automatic replay of completed work are introduced.

## Why This Change Was Made

The earlier checkpoint safeguard ran before the final payload hook. The transport now reapplies the same storage invariant to the final hooked input, including removing a stale continuation reference. Ordinary stored continuation and Azure/custom endpoint policies remain unchanged.

The reply-failure path now uses the existing code-aware format renderer rather than rebuilding a generic diagnostic from the raw error.

OpenAI can report this conflict after streaming output, so this fix prevents the conflicting request rather than retrying after output or tool work has started.

## Evidence

- Before/after regressions reproduce the exact lost-guidance reply and check both the delivered payload and the saved lifecycle notice.
- Serialized-request regressions fail before the fix and pass for SSE, WebSocket, and cached WebSocket, preserving the checkpoint/input and sending only one request.
- **133 focused tests across eight files passed**, including existing continuation, provider-failure, endpoint-policy, and prompt-prefix stability coverage.
- **Live OpenAI API-key proof passed** with a real stored checkpoint: ordinary restoration, reload, and a late-hook override all retain a tool-derived marker across subsequent agent prompts, with one physical request per prompt.
- Scoped TypeScript, lint, formatting, and diff checks passed. No package boundary or dependency changes.
- Independent local autoreview (Codex engine, P0–P2) reviewed the complete candidate against base c5381ef2d215b90a5e5b870543f2c12468f3a66b and reported scoped-clean, with no actionable findings. The local ClawSweeper checkout was outside this session's permitted file scope; the documented autoreview fallback was used. Hosted review remains pending.

The original production request payload was not retained. The late-hook escape is reproduced and fixed, but is not claimed as the confirmed trigger of that particular incident. The affected production conversation has not been reset or resumed as part of this change.

prs.title: fix(media): image descriptions use the ChatGPT OAuth route when OpenAI has no API key
prs.body:
Related: #165961

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: image descriptions fail with `No API key found for provider "openai"` when OpenAI is connected only through ChatGPT OAuth and the Codex plugin is not enabled.

## User Impact

User impact: `view_image` on its configured-model route, inbound image pre-analysis and `openclaw infer image describe` work with a ChatGPT OAuth login. Existing API-key setups and other providers keep their current behavior. No config change or migration is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

A model such as `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` has two routes: the Platform API and ChatGPT. The image runtime resolved the model first, which returned the Platform route, and then asked for credentials scoped to that route. A ChatGPT OAuth profile is rejected on the Platform route, so the request failed before the credential could pick its own route.

The image runtime now uses `prepareSimpleCompletionModel`, the owner that PDF analysis and text completions already use (#156929). It selects the credential first and returns the route that credential owns. This removes the runtime's own auth call, credential-scoped re-resolve, runtime-auth preparation and model binding. Production code is -65 in the image runtime. The shared owner gains two things, in a small sibling module (`simple-completion-credential-model.ts`): it accepts the caller's auth store (the image tool passes the run attempt's store), and an opt-in flag makes it resolve the model again for the account the selected credential belongs to, as the image runtime did before. That re-resolve passes the credential's mode with its profile id, so a profile that only the caller's store holds still works.

The `cloudWorkers.requiredProfile` gate in the shared owner now applies to image descriptions. PDF analysis already goes through the same owner without a worker authority, so image has the same behavior, not a new restriction. The model is also resolved one extra time before auth. The backport to 2026.8.x requested in the issue is a release decision and is not part of this change.

## Evidence

### Runtime output

Setup: one real agent turn (`openclaw agent --local`) in an isolated state directory and OpenClaw home, with a fixture ChatGPT OAuth profile (fake token, no real credential), the Codex plugin disabled, and no OpenAI API key. Three local stubs stand in at the network boundary: a chat model that calls the shipped `view_image` tool, and a TLS stub for `chatgpt.com` and `api.openai.com` that logs which host each request used. The configured image model is `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`.

**Before, on this PR's merge-base `5328b2754d8` (the two changed product files restored to their merge-base content)**

Command:

```sh
sh e2e-165961/run-agent.sh   # builds, writes the fixture profile, starts the stubs, then:
NODE_OPTIONS="--require preload.cjs" pnpm openclaw agent --local --agent main --message "Look at red.png" --json --timeout 120
```

Output (redacted; 4 of about 1070 lines):

```text
[tools] view_image failed: FailoverError: No API key found for provider "openai". You are authenticated with OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex OAuth. Use openai/gpt-6-astra with the ChatGPT/Codex OAuth profile, or set OPENAI_API_KEY for direct OpenAI API access. | missing-provider-auth
== chat stub log
{"at":"2026-11-15T03:46:32.181Z","toolResult":"{\"status\":\"error\",\"tool\":\"view_image\",\"error\":\"No API key found for provider \\\"openai\\\". ..."}"}
== chatgpt/platform stub log (route used by the image model)
(no requests reached the stub)
```

The first line is the tool failing on credential lookup, the second is that error returned to the model as the tool result, and the stub log shows no request left the process.

**After, on this branch (product code identical at `dfe1d5450ea` and the current head `fc0076433b4`; the later commit only deletes a test file)**

Command: the same as above.

Output (redacted; 5 of about 1400 lines):

```text
== chat stub log
{"at":"2026-11-14T22:52:35.500Z","toolResult":"FIXTURE-DESCRIPTION: a small red square on a white background."}
== chatgpt/platform stub log (route used by the image model)
{"at":"2026-11-14T22:52:35.456Z","route":"chatgpt-codex","method":"POST","url":"/backend-api/codex/responses","authScheme":"Bearer","hasAccountHeader":true,"bodyBytes":309}
{"at":"2026-11-14T22:52:35.634Z","route":"platform-api","method":"POST","url":"/v1/embeddings","authScheme":"Bearer","hasAccountHeader":false,"bodyBytes":1158}
```

The second line is the image request leaving on the ChatGPT route (cause), and the first is the tool returning the stub's description (effect). The `platform-api` line is an unrelated background embeddings call from memory indexing, 178 ms later; there is no Platform request for the image. The CLI exits 1 in both runs because the stub chat model's final answer is deliberately minimal; that is a property of the stub.

The same check through the CLI caller, `openclaw infer image describe --file red.png --model openai/gpt-5.6-luna --json`, fails on base with the error above and succeeds with this change on the ChatGPT route.

Not shown: a live run with a real ChatGPT account (fresh OAuth-only setup, or a latest-stable setup upgraded to this change). The ChatGPT route is served by a stub, and `view_image` ran in an embedded agent turn, not in a Gateway process.

### Tests and checks
